I'm glad to see you well.
I have not seen you long. How goes the world?
I haven't seen you for a long time. How is the world treating you?
It wears, sir, as it grows.
It wears out, sir, as it gets older.

Ay, that's well known; / But what particular rarity? what strange, / Which manifold record not matches? See, / Magic of bounty! all these spirits thy power / Hath conjur'd to attend! I know the merchant.

Yes, everyone knows that. But is there anything special, anything strange that no history can match? Look, the magic of generosity! Your power, Timon's bounty, has conjured all these people here to wait on him. I know the merchant.
I know them both; th' other's a jeweller.
I know them both. The other one is a jeweller.
A most incomparable man; breath'd, as it were, / To an untirable and continuate goodness. / He passes.
A man beyond comparison, trained, you might say, to a tireless and never-ending goodness. He surpasses everyone.
O, pray let's see't: for the Lord Timon, sir?
Oh, please let me see it. Is it for Lord Timon, sir?
If he will touch the estimate: but for that—
If he will pay what it's worth. But as for that...
When we for recompense have prais'd the vile, / It stains the glory in that happy verse / Which aptly sings the good.
(Reciting to himself) When we praise wicked men in return for payment, it spoils the glory of the poem that rightly celebrates the good.
[Looking at the jewel] 'Tis a good form.
(Looking at the jewel) It's a well-shaped stone.
And rich: here is a water, look ye.
And a rich one. Look at the clear sparkle in it.
You are rapt, sir, in some work, some dedication / To the great lord.
You're lost in thought, sir, working on some poem, some dedication to the great lord.

A thing slipp'd idly from me. / Our poesy is as a gum, which oozes / From whence 'tis nourish'd: the fire i' the flint / Shows not till it be struck; our gentle flame / Provokes itself, and like the current flies / Each bound it chafes. What have you there?

Just something that slipped out of me without effort. Poetry is like the gum that oozes from a tree where it grows. The fire in a flint doesn't show until it's struck, but our gentle flame lights itself and, like a running stream, flows past each bank that holds it in. What have you got there?
A picture, sir. When comes your book forth?
A picture, sir. When is your book coming out?
Upon the heels of my presentment, sir. / Let's see your piece.
As soon as I've presented it to Timon, sir. Let me see your painting.
So 'tis: this comes off well and excellent.
So it is. This has come out excellently.
Admirable! How this grace / Speaks his own standing! what a mental power / This eye shoots forth! how big imagination / Moves in this lip! to the dumbness of the gesture / One might interpret.
It's wonderful! See how the figure's grace shows his high rank! What power of mind shines from this eye! What great imagination moves in this lip! You could put words to the silent gesture.
It is a pretty mocking of the life. / Here is a touch; is't good?
It's a fair imitation of life. Here's a touch of detail. Is it good?
I'll say of it, / It tutors nature: artificial strife / Lives in these touches, livelier than life.
I'll say this of it: it teaches nature a lesson. Art competing with nature lives in these brushstrokes, more lifelike than life itself.
How many people follow this lord!
The senators of Athens: happy man!
Those are the senators of Athens. Lucky man!

You see this confluence, this great flood of visitors. / I have, in this rough work, shap'd out a man / Whom this beneath world doth embrace and hug / With amplest entertainment: my free drift / Halts not particularly, but moves itself / In a wide sea of wax: no levell'd malice / Infects one comma in the course I hold: / But flies an eagle flight, bold and forth on, / Leaving no tract behind.

You see this crowd, this great flood of visitors. In this rough draft I have shaped a man whom the whole world below heaven embraces and welcomes most warmly. My poem's free movement doesn't stop at any one person but ranges over a wide sea of subjects. No pointed malice infects a single comma of it. It flies boldly onward like an eagle and leaves no trail behind.
What do you mean by that?

I will unbolt to you. / You see how all conditions, how all minds— / As well of glib and slipp'ry creatures as / Of grave and austere quality—tender down / Their services to Lord Timon: his large fortune, / Upon his good and gracious nature hanging, / Subdues and properties to his love and tendance / All sorts of hearts; yea, from the glass-fac'd flatterer / To Apemantus, that few things loves better / Than to abhor himself: even he drops down / The knee before him, and returns in peace / Most rich in Timon's nod.

I'll explain. You see how men of every rank and every temper, the smooth and slippery ones as well as the serious and strict, offer their services to Lord Timon. His great fortune, joined to his good and gracious nature, wins over every kind of heart and makes it his to love and serve. Yes, from the flatterer whose face is a mirror of his patron's, to Apemantus, who loves almost nothing better than hating himself. Even he kneels to Timon, and goes away content, rich in a nod from him.

Sir, I have upon a high and pleasant hill / Feign'd Fortune to be thron'd: the base o' the mount / Is rank'd with all deserts, all kind of natures / That labour on the bosom of this sphere / To propagate their states: amongst them all, / Whose eyes are on this sovereign lady fix'd / One do I personate of Lord Timon's frame, / Whom Fortune with her ivory hand wafts to her; / Whose present grace to present slaves and servants / Translates his rivals.

Sir, in my poem I have imagined Fortune sitting on a throne on top of a high and pleasant hill. The bottom of the hill is crowded with people of every merit and every nature who toil on this earth to improve their position. Among all those whose eyes are fixed on this sovereign lady, I portray one man like Lord Timon, whom Fortune beckons up to her with her ivory hand. Her favour instantly turns his rivals into his slaves and servants.

'Tis conceiv'd to scope. / This throne, this Fortune, and this hill, methinks, / With one man beckon'd from the rest below, / Bowing his head against the steepy mount / To climb his happiness, would be well express'd / In our condition.

That's well imagined. This throne, this Fortune and this hill, with one man called up from the rest below, bowing his head as he climbs the steep slope to his happiness, would make a fine painting in my art.

Nay, sir, but hear me on. / All those which were his fellows but of late, / Some better than his value, on the moment / Follow his strides, his lobbies fill with tendance, / Rain sacrificial whisperings in his ear, / Make sacred even his stirrup, and through him / Drink the free air.

No, sir, hear the rest. All those who were his equals only lately, some of them worth more than he was, at once follow in his footsteps. They fill his halls with their attendance, pour flattering whispers into his ear as if they were prayers, treat even his stirrup as holy, and breathe the free air only through him.
Yes, of course. What about them?

When Fortune in her shift and change of mood / Spurns down her late beloved, all his dependants, / Which labour'd after him to the mountain's top / Even on their knees and hands, let him slip down, / Not one accompanying his declining foot.

When Fortune changes her mood and kicks down her recent favourite, all his followers, who crawled after him to the top of the mountain on their hands and knees, let him slide down. Not one of them goes with him on the way down.

'Tis common: / A thousand moral paintings I can show / That shall demonstrate these quick blows of Fortune's / More pregnantly than words. Yet you do well / To show Lord Timon that mean eyes have seen / The foot above the head.

That's a common theme. I could show you a thousand moral paintings that show these sudden blows of Fortune more powerfully than words. Still, you do well to show Lord Timon that humble people have seen the mighty fall.
Ay, my good lord. Five talents is his debt, / His means most short, his creditors most strait: / Your honourable letter he desires / To those have shut him up; which, failing, / Periods his comfort.

Yes, my good lord. His debt is five talents, his money is very short, and his creditors very strict. He asks you to write a letter to the men who have locked him up. If you don't, his hopes are at an end.

Noble Ventidius! Well: / I am not of that feather to shake off / My friend when he must need me. I do know him / A gentleman that well deserves a help, / Which he shall have: I'll pay the debt and free him.
Noble Ventidius! Well, I'm not the kind of bird to shake off a friend just when he needs me. I know him to be a gentleman who deserves help, and he shall have it. I'll pay the debt and set him free.
Your lordship puts him in your debt forever.
Commend me to him; I will send his ransom; / And being enfranchis'd, bid him come to me. / 'Tis not enough to help the feeble up, / But to support him after. Fare you well.
Give him my regards. I will send the money to free him, and once he's released, tell him to come to me. It isn't enough to help a weak man to his feet; you must support him afterwards too. Goodbye.
I wish your honour every happiness.
Thou hast a servant nam'd Lucilius.
You have a servant called Lucilius.
I have so: what of him?
Most noble Timon, call the man before thee.
Most noble Timon, call the man here.
Attends he here or no? Lucilius!
Is he here or not? Lucilius!

This fellow here, Lord Timon, this thy creature, / By night frequents my house. I am a man / That from my first have been inclin'd to thrift, / And my estate deserves an heir more rais'd / Than one which holds a trencher.

This fellow here, Lord Timon, this servant of yours, visits my house at night. I am a man who has been careful with money all my life, and my estate deserves a more important heir than a man who waits at table.

One only daughter have I, no kin else, / On whom I may confer what I have got: / The maid is fair, o' the youngest for a bride, / And I have bred her at my dearest cost / In qualities of the best. This man of thine / Attempts her love: I prithee, noble lord, / Join with me to forbid him her resort; / Myself have spoke in vain.

I have only one daughter and no other family to leave what I've earned to. The girl is pretty, just old enough to be a bride, and I have raised her at great cost with the best accomplishments. This man of yours is trying to win her love. Please, noble lord, help me forbid him to see her. I have told him myself, with no result.
Therefore he will be, Timon: / His honesty rewards him in itself; / It must not bear my daughter.
Then let him stay honest, Timon. His honesty is its own reward. It shouldn't win him my daughter as well.
She is young and apt: / Our own precedent passions do instruct us / What levity's in youth.
She is young and easily swayed. Our own past passions teach us how giddy the young can be.
(To Lucilius) Do you love the girl?
Ay, my good lord, and she accepts of it.
Yes, my good lord, and she returns my love.
If in her marriage my consent be missing, / I call the gods to witness, I will choose / Mine heir from forth the beggars of the world, / And dispossess her all.
If she marries without my consent, I swear by the gods I'll choose my heir from among the world's beggars and leave her nothing.
How shall she be endow'd, / If she be mated with an equal husband?
What dowry will she have if she marries a man of equal rank?
Three talents on the present; in future, all.
Three talents now, and everything I own later.

This gentleman of mine hath serv'd me long: / To build his fortune I will strain a little, / For 'tis a bond in men. Give him thy daughter: / What you bestow, in him I'll counterpoise, / And make him weigh with her.

This gentleman has served me for a long time. I will stretch myself a little to make his fortune, because that is a duty between men. Give him your daughter. Whatever you give her, I'll give him the same, so that he will be her equal.
Most noble lord, / Pawn me to this your honour, she is his.
Most noble lord, give me your word of honour on it and she is his.
My hand to thee; mine honour on my promise.
Here is my hand, and my honour stands behind my promise.
Humbly I thank your lordship. Never may / That state or fortune fall into my keeping / Which is not owed to you!
I humbly thank your lordship. May I never own any wealth or rank that I do not owe to you!
[Presenting his poem] Vouchsafe my labour, and long live your lordship!
(Presenting his poem) Please accept my work, and long live your lordship!
I thank you; you shall hear from me anon: / Go not away. What have you there, my friend?
Thank you. You'll hear from me soon. Don't go away. What have you got there, my friend?
A piece of painting, which I do beseech / Your lordship to accept.
A painting, which I beg your lordship to accept.

Painting is welcome. / The painting is almost the natural man; / For since dishonour traffics with man's nature, / He is but outside: these pencill'd figures are / Even such as they give out. I like your work; / And you shall find I like it: wait attendance / Till you hear further from me.

A painting is welcome. A painting is almost a real man. Since dishonesty became part of human nature, man is all outward show, but these painted figures are exactly what they appear to be. I like your work, and you'll see that I mean it. Wait here until you hear more from me.
Well fare you, gentleman: give me your hand; / We must needs dine together. Sir, your jewel / Hath suffered under praise.
Goodbye, sir. Give me your hand; we must dine together. Sir, your jewel has suffered from praise.
What, my lord? Has it been criticised?
A mere satiety of commendations; / If I should pay you for 't as 'tis extoll'd, / It would unclew me quite.
No, it has been praised to excess. If I paid you for it at the price it's been praised at, it would ruin me completely.

My lord, 'tis rated / As those which sell would give: but you well know, / Things of like value, differing in the owners, / Are prized by their masters. Believe't, dear lord, / You mend the jewel by the wearing it.

My lord, it's priced at what the sellers would pay themselves. But you know that things of equal value are prized according to who owns them. Believe me, dear lord, you make the jewel better by wearing it.
No, my good lord; he speaks the common tongue, / Which all men speak with him.
No, my good lord, he only says what everybody says.
Look who comes here. Will you be chid?
Look who's coming. Are you ready to be scolded?
We'll bear it along with your lordship.
Good morrow to thee, gentle Apemantus!
Good morning to you, gentle Apemantus!
Till I be gentle, stay thou for thy good morrow; / When thou art Timon's dog, and these knaves honest.
Wait for me to wish you good morning until I am gentle, which will be when you are turned into Timon's dog and these rogues are honest.
Why dost thou call them knaves? thou know'st them not.
Why do you call them rogues? You don't know them.
Then I don't take it back.
Thou know'st I do; I call'd thee by thy name.
You know I do. I called you by your name: rogue.
Of nothing so much as that I am not like Timon.
Of nothing so much as of not being like Timon.
To knock out an honest Athenian's brains.
To knock out an honest Athenian's brains.
That's a deed thou'lt die for.
That's a crime you'll be executed for.
Right, if doing nothing be death by the law.
True, if doing nothing is punishable by death. There are no honest Athenians to kill.
How likest thou this picture, Apemantus?
What do you think of this picture, Apemantus?
It's the best thing here, because it is innocent: it can do no harm.
Wrought he not well that painted it?
Didn't the man who painted it do good work?
He wrought better that made the painter; and yet he's / but a filthy piece of work.
The one who made the painter did better work, and even he is a filthy piece of work.
Thy mother's of my generation: what's she, if I be a dog?
Your mother is of my kind. What is she, if I'm a dog?
Will you dine with me, Apemantus?
An thou shouldst, thou'dst anger ladies.
If you did, you'd make the ladies angry.
O! they eat lords; so they come by great bellies.
Oh, they eat lords, and that's how they get big bellies.
That's a dirty way of taking it.
So thou apprehendest it, take it for thy labour.
It's your understanding that took it that way, so keep it as your reward.
How dost thou like this jewel, Apemantus?
What do you think of this jewel, Apemantus?
Not so well as plain dealing, which will not cost a man / a doit.
Not as much as I think of honest dealing, which doesn't cost a man a penny.
What do you think it's worth?
Not worth my thinking. How now, poet!
Not worth thinking about. Hello, poet!
Then thou liest: look in thy last work, where thou hast / feigned him a worthy fellow.
Then you are lying. Look at your latest work, where you have pretended he is a worthy man.
That's not feigned; he is so.
That isn't pretence. He is worthy.
Yes, he is worthy of thee, and to pay thee for thy / labour: he that loves to be flattered is worthy o' the flatterer. / Heavens, that I were a lord!
Yes, he is worthy of you, and worthy to pay you for your work. A man who loves to be flattered deserves the flatterer. Heavens, I wish I were a lord!
What would you do then, Apemantus?
Even as Apemantus does now; hate a lord with my heart.
Just what Apemantus does now: hate a lord with all my heart.
That I had no angry wit to be a lord. Art not thou a merchant?
For having had no better sense than to become a lord. Aren't you a merchant?
Traffic confound thee, if the gods will not!
May trade ruin you, if the gods won't!
If traffic do it, the gods do it.
If trade ruins me, it will be the gods doing it.
Traffic's thy god, and thy god confound thee!
Trade is your god, and may your god ruin you!
'Tis Alcibiades, and some twenty horse, / All of companionship.
It's Alcibiades, with about twenty horsemen, all his companions.
Pray entertain them; give them guide to us.
Please welcome them and bring them to us.
You must needs dine with me. Go not you hence / Till I have thank'd you; when dinner's done, / Show me this piece. I am joyful of your sights.
You must dine with me. Don't leave until I've thanked you. When dinner is over, show me this painting. I'm delighted to see you all.

So, so, there! / Aches contract and starve your supple joints! / That there should be small love 'mongst these sweet knaves, / And all this courtesy! The strain of man's bred out / Into baboon and monkey.

There, look at that! May aches shrink and wither your bending joints! To think there's so little love among these charming rogues, and all this politeness! The human race has degenerated into baboons and monkeys.
Sir, you have sav'd my longing, and I feed / Most hungerly on your sight.
Sir, you have satisfied my longing to see you, and I feast hungrily on the sight of you.
Right welcome, sir! / Ere we depart we'll share a bounteous time / In different pleasures. Pray you, let us in.
You are very welcome, sir! Before we part we'll share a fine time with all kinds of pleasures. Please, let's go in.
What time o' day is't, Apemantus?
What time of day is it, Apemantus?
The more accursed thou that still omitt'st it.
Then you are all the more damned for always missing it.
Thou art going to Lord Timon's feast.
You're going to Lord Timon's feast.
Ay; to see meat fill knaves and wine heat fools.
Yes, to see food fill rogues and wine heat up fools.
Fare thee well, fare thee well.
Thou art a fool to bid me farewell twice.
You're a fool to say goodbye to me twice.
Shouldst have kept one to thyself, for I mean to give thee none.
You should have kept one for yourself, because I'm not going to give you any.
No, I will do nothing at thy bidding: make thy requests to thy / friend.
No, I won't do anything you tell me to. Make your requests to your friend.
Away, unpeaceable dog! or I'll spurn thee hence.
Go away, you quarrelsome dog, or I'll kick you out of here.
I will fly, like a dog, the heels of an ass.
I'll run from the heels of an ass, as a dog does.
He's opposite to humanity. Come, shall we in, / And taste Lord Timon's bounty? he outgoes / The very heart of kindness.
He's the enemy of all humanity. Come, shall we go in and enjoy Lord Timon's generosity? He goes beyond kindness itself.
He pours it out; Plutus, the god of gold, / Is but his steward: no meed but he repays / Sevenfold above itself; no gift to him / But breeds the giver a return exceeding / All use of quittance.
He pours it out. Plutus, the god of wealth, is only his steward. He repays every favour seven times over, and nobody gives him a gift without getting back far more than any normal repayment.
The noblest mind he carries / That ever govern'd man.
He has the noblest mind that ever ruled a man.
Long may he live in fortunes! Shall we in?
May he live long and prosper! Shall we go in?

Most honour'd Timon, / It hath pleas'd the gods to remember my father's age, / And call him to long peace. / He is gone happy, and has left me rich: / Then, as in grateful virtue I am bound / To your free heart, I do return those talents, / Doubled with thanks and service, from whose help / I deriv'd liberty.

Most honoured Timon, the gods have been pleased to remember my father's old age and call him to his long rest. He has died happy and left me rich. So, since gratitude binds me to your generous heart, I return those talents that bought my freedom, doubled, with my thanks and service.

O! by no means, / Honest Ventidius: you mistake my love; / I gave it freely ever; and there's none / Can truly say he gives, if he receives: / If our betters play at that game, we must not dare / To imitate them; faults that are rich are fair.

Oh, certainly not, honest Ventidius. You misunderstand my love. I always gave freely, and nobody can truly say he gives if he takes something back. If our superiors play that game, we must not dare copy them. Rich men's faults are always called fair.

Nay, my lords, ceremony was but devis'd at first / To set a gloss on faint deeds, hollow welcomes, / Recanting goodness, sorry ere 'tis shown; / But where there is true friendship there needs none. / Pray, sit; more welcome are ye to my fortunes / Than my fortunes to me.

No, my lords, ceremony was first invented to put a shine on half-hearted deeds, empty welcomes, and kindness that is regretted even before it is shown. Where there is true friendship, none is needed. Please, sit down. You are more welcome to my wealth than my wealth is to me.
My lord, we always have confess'd it.
My lord, we have always admitted it.
Ho, ho! confess'd it; hang'd it, have you not?
Ha! Admitted it? You'll be hanged for it, won't you?
No, / You shall not make me welcome: / I come to have thee thrust me out of doors.
No, you won't make me welcome. I've come so that you can throw me out.

Fie! thou'rt a churl; ye've got a humour there / Does not become a man; 'tis much to blame. / They say, my lords, Ira furor brevis est; / But yond man is ever angry. / Go, let him have a table by himself; / For he does neither affect company, / Nor is he fit for it, indeed.

For shame, you're a boor. You have a mood that doesn't suit a man; it's very wrong. They say, my lords, "anger is a short madness", but that man is always angry. Go, give him a table of his own, because he doesn't like company and isn't fit for it either.
Let me stay at thine apperil, Timon: / I come to observe; I give thee warning on't.
Let me stay at your own risk, Timon. I've come to watch. I'm warning you.
I take no heed of thee; thou'rt an Athenian, therefore, welcome. / I myself would have no power; prithee; let my meat make thee / silent.
I pay no attention to you. You're an Athenian, so you're welcome. I don't want the power to silence you myself; please, let my food silence you.

I scorn thy meat; 't'would choke me, for I should / Ne'er flatter thee. O you gods! what a number / Of men eats Timon, and he sees 'em not! / It grieves me to see so many dip their meat / In one man's blood; and all the madness is, / He cheers them up too. / I wonder men dare trust themselves with men: / Methinks they should invite them without knives; / Good for their meat, and safer for their lives. / There's much example for 't; the fellow that / Sits next him now, parts bread with him, pledges / The breath of him in a divided draught, / Is the readiest man to kill him: 't has been prov'd. / If I were a huge man, I should fear to drink at meals; / Lest they should spy my wind-pipe's dangerous notes: / Great men should drink with harness on their throats.

I despise your food. It would choke me, because I would never flatter you to earn it. Oh you gods, how many men are eating Timon, and he doesn't see it! It upsets me to see so many dip their bread in one man's blood, and the maddest part of it is that he encourages them. I'm amazed that men dare trust themselves with other men. I think they should invite guests without knives: it would be good for the food and safer for their lives. There are plenty of examples. The fellow sitting next to him now, sharing his bread and drinking his health from the same cup, is the man readiest to kill him. It has been proved before. If I were a great man I'd be afraid to drink at meals, in case they spotted where my windpipe was weakest. Great men should drink with armour on their throats.
My lord, in heart; and let the health go round.
(Drinking a toast) My lord, with all my heart, and let the toast go round.
Let it flow this way, my good lord.
Let it come this way, my good lord.

Flow this way! A brave fellow! he keeps his tides well. Those / healths will make thee and thy state look ill, Timon. / Here's that which is too weak to be a sinner, / Honest water, which ne'er left man i' the mire: / This and my food are equals; there's no odds: / Feasts are too proud to give thanks to the gods. / Immortal gods, I crave no pelf; / I pray for no man but myself. / Grant I may never prove so fond / To trust man on his oath or bond; / Or a harlot for her weeping; / Or a dog that seems a-sleeping; / Or a keeper with my freedom; / Or my friends, if I should need 'em. / Amen. So fall to't. / Rich men sin, and I eat root.

"Come this way"! What a fine fellow! He knows how to catch the tide. Those toasts will make you and your fortune look sick, Timon. Here's something too weak to make anyone sin: honest water, which never left a man in the mud. This and my food are equal partners. Feasts are too proud to thank the gods. (Saying grace) Immortal gods, I don't ask for money. I pray for nobody but myself. Grant that I may never be so foolish as to trust a man's oath or his signed promise, or a prostitute's tears, or a dog that seems to be asleep, or a jailer with my freedom, or my friends if I should need them. Amen. So, tuck in. Rich men sin, and I eat roots.
Much good dich thy good heart, Apemantus!
Much good may it do your good heart, Apemantus!
Captain Alcibiades, your heart's in the field now.
Captain Alcibiades, your heart is on the battlefield now.
My heart is ever at your service, my lord.
My heart is always at your service, my lord.
You had rather be at a breakfast of enemies than a dinner of / friends.
You'd rather be at a breakfast of enemies than a dinner of friends.
So they were bleeding-new, my lord, there's no meat / like 'em: I could wish my best friend at such a feast.
As long as they were freshly bleeding, my lord, there's no meat like them. I could wish my best friend at a feast like that.
'Would all those flatterers were thine enemies then, that / then thou mightst kill 'em, and bid me to 'em.
Then I wish all those flatterers were your enemies, so that you could kill them and invite me to eat them.
Might we but have that happiness, my lord, that you / would once use our hearts, whereby we might express some part of / our zeals, we should think ourselves for ever perfect.
If only we might have the happiness, my lord, of your using our hearts some day, so that we could show some part of our devotion, we would think ourselves perfectly content forever.

O, no doubt, my good friends, but the gods themselves have / provided that I shall have much help from you: how had you been / my friends else? why have you that charitable title from / thousands, did not you chiefly belong to my heart? I have told / more of you to myself than you can with modesty speak in your own / behalf; and thus far I confirm you. O you gods! think I, what / need we have any friends if we should ne'er have need of 'em? / they were the most needless creatures living, should we ne'er / have use for 'em; and would most resemble sweet instruments hung / up in cases, that keep their sounds to themselves. Why, I have / often wished myself poorer that I might come nearer to you. We / are born to do benefits; and what better or properer can we call / our own than the riches of our friends? O! what a precious / comfort 'tis to have so many, like brothers, commanding one / another's fortunes! O joy! e'en made away ere it can be born. / Mine eyes cannot hold out water, methinks: to forget their / faults, I drink to you.

Oh, I'm sure, my good friends, that the gods themselves have arranged for me to have a lot of help from you. How else would you be my friends? Why else would you, out of thousands, be called friends, unless you belonged above all to my heart? I have said more good of you to myself than you could modestly say of yourselves, and to that extent I'm sure of you. "Oh you gods," I think, "what need would we have of any friends if we never needed them? They would be the most useless creatures alive if we never had any use for them. They would be like sweet instruments hung up in their cases, keeping their music to themselves." Why, I have often wished I were poorer so that I could come closer to you. We are born to do good to others, and what can we more truly call our own than our friends' riches? Oh, what a precious comfort it is to have so many friends who, like brothers, can command each other's fortunes! Oh joy, spilling over before it can even be born! My eyes can't hold back their tears. To cover up their weakness, I drink to you.
Thou weepest to make them drink, Timon.
You're crying so you can make them drink, Timon.
Joy had the like conception in our eyes, / And, at that instant like a babe, sprung up.
Joy was conceived in our eyes the same way, and at that moment was born like a baby: in tears.
Ho, ho! I laugh to think that babe a bastard.
Ha! It makes me laugh to think that baby is a bastard.
I promise you, my lord, you mov'd me much.
I promise you, my lord, you moved me deeply.
Please you, my lord, there are certain ladies most desirous of / admittance.
If you please, my lord, there are some ladies who very much want to come in.
There comes with them a forerunner, my lord, which bears / that office, to signify their pleasures.
They have sent a messenger ahead of them, my lord, whose job is to explain what they wish.
I pray, let them be admitted.

Hail to thee, worthy Timon; and to all / That of his bounties taste! The five best Senses / Acknowledge thee their patron; and come freely / To gratulate thy plenteous bosom. Th' Ear, / Taste, Touch, Smell, pleas'd from thy table rise; / They only now come but to feast thine eyes.

Greetings to you, worthy Timon, and to everyone who enjoys his generosity! The five senses acknowledge you as their patron and come of their own accord to praise your generous heart. Hearing, taste, touch and smell rise satisfied from your table. Now they have only come to feast your eyes.
They are welcome all; let 'em have kind admittance: / Music, make their welcome!
They are all welcome. Let them in kindly. Music, welcome them!
You see, my lord, how ample you're belov'd.
You see, my lord, how widely you are loved.

Hoy-day! what a sweep of vanity comes this way: / They dance! they are mad women. / Like madness is the glory of this life, / As this pomp shows to a little oil and root. / We make ourselves fools to disport ourselves; / And spend our flatteries to drink those men / Upon whose age we void it up again, / With poisonous spite and envy. / Who lives that's not depraved or depraves? / Who dies that bears not one spurn to their graves / Of their friend's gift? / I should fear those that dance before me now / Would one day stamp upon me: it has been done: / Men shut their doors against a setting sun.

Well, well! What a parade of vanity is coming this way! They're dancing! They're mad women. The glory of this life is just as mad as this display looks next to a meal of a little oil and roots. We make fools of ourselves to entertain ourselves, and waste our flattery toasting men whom, when they're old, we spit back out with poisonous spite and envy. Who lives who isn't corrupted or corrupting others? Who dies without taking to the grave some kick given by a friend? I'd be afraid that the women dancing in front of me now would one day stamp on me. It has happened before: men shut their doors on a setting sun.

You have done our pleasures much grace, fair ladies, / Set a fair fashion on our entertainment, / Which was not half so beautiful and kind; / You have added worth unto 't and lustre, / And entertain'd me with mine own device; / I am to thank you for 't.

You have greatly honoured our pleasures, fair ladies. You've decorated our entertainment, which wasn't half so beautiful and charming before. You've given it worth and shine, and entertained me with my own idea. I must thank you for it.
My lord, you take us even at the best.
My lord, you take us at our very best.
Faith, for the worst is filthy; and would not hold taking, I / doubt me.
Yes, because the worst of them is filthy, and wouldn't bear taking, I suspect.
Ladies, there is an idle banquet / Attends you; please you to dispose yourselves.
Ladies, a light dessert is waiting for you. Please help yourselves.
The little casket bring me hither.
Bring me the little jewel box.

Yes, my lord. [Aside] More jewels yet! / There is no crossing him in 's humour; / Else I should tell him well, i' faith, I should, / When all's spent, he'd be cross'd then, an he could. / 'Tis pity bounty had not eyes behind, / That man might ne'er be wretched for his mind.

Yes, my lord. (Aside) More jewels! There's no stopping him when he's in this mood. Otherwise I would tell him plainly, I really would. When it's all spent, he'd want to be stopped then, if he could. It's a pity generosity doesn't have eyes in the back of its head, so that a man would never be ruined by his own good nature.
O, my friends! I have one word to say to you; / Look you, my good lord, / I must entreat you, honour me so much / As to advance this jewel; accept it and wear it, / Kind my lord.
Oh, my friends, I have one more word to say to you. Look, my good lord, I must ask you to do me the honour of improving this jewel by accepting it and wearing it, my kind lord.
I am so far already in your gifts—
I already owe you so much in gifts...
My lord, there are certain nobles of the Senate / Newly alighted and come to visit you.
My lord, some noblemen of the Senate have just dismounted and have come to visit you.
I beseech your honour, / Vouchsafe me a word; it does concern you near.
I beg your honour, allow me a word. It concerns you closely.
Near! why then, another time I'll hear thee. / I prithee let's be provided to show them entertainment.
Closely? Then I'll hear you some other time. Please, let's get ready to entertain them.
May it please your honour, Lord Lucius, / Out of his free love, hath presented to you / Four milk-white horses, trapp'd in silver.
If it please your honour, Lord Lucius, out of pure friendship, has sent you four milk-white horses, harnessed in silver.
I shall accept them fairly; let the presents / Be worthily entertain'd.
I'll accept them gladly. See that the gifts are properly looked after.
Please you, my lord, that honourable gentleman, Lord Lucullus, / entreats your company to-morrow to hunt with him, and has sent / your honour two brace of greyhounds.
If you please, my lord, that honourable gentleman Lord Lucullus asks you to hunt with him tomorrow, and has sent your honour two pairs of greyhounds.
I'll hunt with him; and let them be receiv'd, / Not without fair reward.
I'll hunt with him. Receive the dogs, and give a generous reward for them.

[Aside] What will this come to? / He commands us to provide, and give great gifts, / And all out of an empty coffer; / Nor will he know his purse, or yield me this, / To show him what a beggar his heart is, / Being of no power to make his wishes good. / His promises fly so beyond his state / That what he speaks is all in debt; he owes / For every word: he is so kind that he now / Pays interest for 't; his land's put to their books. / Well, would I were gently put out of office / Before I were forc'd out! / Happier he that has no friend to feed / Than such that do e'en enemies exceed. / I bleed inwardly for my lord.

(Aside) Where will this end? He orders us to provide feasts and give great gifts, all out of an empty money chest. He won't find out how much is in his purse, or let me show him what a beggar his heart has become, since it has no power to make its wishes come true. His promises go so far beyond his means that everything he says is in debt. He owes for every word. He is so kind that he now pays interest on his kindness. His lands are mortgaged in his creditors' account books. Well, I wish I could be gently retired from my job before I'm forced out of it! A man with no friends to feed is happier than one whose friends are worse than enemies. I'm bleeding inside for my lord.
You do yourselves much wrong; / You bate too much of your own merits; / Here, my lord, a trifle of our love.
You do yourselves an injustice; you underrate your own merits. Here, my lord, a small token of my love.
With more than common thanks I will receive it.
I accept it with more than ordinary thanks.
O! he's the very soul of bounty!
Oh, he's the very soul of generosity!
And now I remember, my lord, you gave / Good words the other day of a bay courser / I rode on: it is yours because you lik'd it.
And now I remember, my lord, you spoke well the other day of a bay horse I was riding. It's yours, because you liked it.
O! I beseech you, pardon me, my lord, in that.
Oh, please excuse me from that, my lord.
You may take my word, my lord: I know no man / Can justly praise but what he does affect: / I weigh my friend's affection with mine own. / I'll tell you true; I'll call to you.
You can take my word for it, my lord: I know no man truly praises anything unless he wants it. I value my friend's desire as I value my own. I'm telling you the truth. I'll call on you.
Oh, nobody would be so welcome!

I take all and your several visitations / So kind to heart, 'tis not enough to give; / Methinks, I could deal kingdoms to my friends, / And ne'er be weary. Alcibiades, / Thou art a soldier, therefore seldom rich; / It comes in charity to thee; for all thy living / Is 'mongst the dead, and all the lands thou hast / Lie in a pitch'd field.

I take all your visits so kindly to heart that giving isn't enough. I feel I could hand out kingdoms to my friends and never grow tired. Alcibiades, you're a soldier, and so seldom rich. It's charity to give to you, because your whole income comes from the dead, and all the land you own is battlefields.
Yes, land soiled with blood, my lord.
We are so deeply obliged to you...
And so am I to you.
And so am I to you.
All to you. Lights, more lights!
I'm entirely yours. Lights, more lights!
The best of happiness, / Honour, and fortunes, keep with you, Lord Timon!
May the greatest happiness, honour and fortune stay with you, Lord Timon!
And always ready for his friends.

What a coil's here! / Serving of becks and jutting out of bums! / I doubt whether their legs be worth the sums / That are given for 'em. Friendship's full of dregs: / Methinks, false hearts should never have sound legs. / Thus honest fools lay out their wealth on curtsies.

What a fuss there is here! Bowing and scraping and sticking out of bottoms! I doubt whether their bending legs are worth the sums paid for them. Friendship is full of dregs. It seems to me that false hearts should never have healthy legs. That's how honest fools spend their wealth on bows.
Now, Apemantus, if thou wert not sullen, / I would be good to thee.
Now, Apemantus, if you weren't so sulky, I would be generous to you.

No, I'll nothing; for if I should be bribed too, there / would be none left to rail upon thee, and then thou wouldst sin / the faster. Thou givest so long, Timon, I fear me thou wilt give / away thyself in paper shortly: What needs these feasts, pomps, / and vain-glories?

No, I'll take nothing. If I were bribed too, there would be nobody left to criticise you, and then you would sin all the faster. You give so much, Timon, that I'm afraid you'll soon give yourself away in IOUs. What's the need for these feasts, this pomp and empty show?
Nay, an you begin to rail on society once, I am sworn not to / give regard to you. Farewell; and come with better music.
No, if you're going to start attacking good company, I've sworn not to listen to you. Goodbye, and come back with a better tune.
So: Thou wilt not hear me now; thou shalt not then; / I'll lock thy heaven from thee. / O! that men's ears should be / To counsel deaf, but not to flattery!
So, you won't hear me now. Then you shan't hear me later, when you need to. I'll lock your heaven away from you. Oh, that men's ears should be deaf to good advice but not to flattery!

And late, five thousand: to Varro and to Isidore / He owes nine thousand; besides my former sum, / Which makes it five-and-twenty. Still in motion / Of raging waste! It cannot hold; it will not. / If I want gold, steal but a beggar's dog / And give it Timon, why, the dog coins gold; / If I would sell my horse, and buy twenty more / Better than he, why, give my horse to Timon, / Ask nothing, give it him, it foals me straight, / And able horses. No porter at his gate, / But rather one that smiles and still invites / All that pass by. It cannot hold; no reason / Can found his state in safety. Caphis, ho! / Caphis, I say!

And recently five thousand. He owes Varro and Isidore nine thousand, besides the sum I lent him before, which makes it twenty-five thousand. And still he goes on wasting madly! It can't last, it won't. If I want gold, I need only steal a beggar's dog and give it to Timon, and the dog turns into gold. If I wanted to sell my horse and buy twenty better ones, I need only give my horse to Timon, asking nothing, and straight away it gives birth to fine grown horses for me. There's no porter at his gate to keep people out, only one who smiles and invites in everyone who passes. It can't last. No reasoning can find his fortune safe. Caphis, hey! Caphis, I say!
Here, sir; what is your pleasure?
Here, sir. What do you want?

Get on your cloak, and haste you to Lord Timon; / Importune him for my moneys; be not ceas'd / With slight denial, nor then silenc'd when— / 'Commend me to your master'—and the cap / Plays in the right hand, thus;—but tell him, / My uses cry to me; I must serve my turn / Out of mine own; his days and times are past, / And my reliances on his fracted dates / Have smit my credit: I love and honour him, / But must not break my back to heal his finger; / Immediate are my needs, and my relief / Must not be toss'd and turn'd to me in words, / But find supply immediate. Get you gone: / Put on a most importunate aspect, / A visage of demand; for I do fear, / When every feather sticks in his own wing, / Lord Timon will be left a naked gull, / Which flashes now a phoenix. Get you gone.

Put on your cloak and hurry to Lord Timon. Press him for my money. Don't be put off by a feeble refusal, or silenced when he says "Give my regards to your master" while twirling his hat in his right hand, like this. Tell him my needs are calling for it; I have to serve my own turn out of my own money. His payment dates have passed, and by relying on his broken promises I've damaged my own credit. I love and honour him, but I can't break my own back to heal his finger. My needs are urgent, and my relief mustn't be tossed back to me in words; it must come at once. Go. Put on a most demanding face, the look of a man asking for what he's owed. I'm afraid that when every borrowed feather is back in its own bird's wing, Lord Timon, who now shines like a phoenix, will be left a naked, plucked fool.
Take the bonds along with you, / And have the dates in compt.
Take the bonds with you, and have the dates worked out.

No care, no stop! So senseless of expense, / That he will neither know how to maintain it, / Nor cease his flow of riot: takes no account / How things go from him, nor resumes no care / Of what is to continue: never mind / Was to be so unwise, to be so kind. / What shall be done? He will not hear, till feel: / I must be round with him. Now he comes from hunting. / Fie, fie, fie, fie!

No caution, no stopping! He's so unaware of what he spends that he neither knows how to pay for it nor will stop his flood of extravagance. He takes no notice of how things slip away from him, and gives no thought to how he'll carry on. Never was a mind so unwise as to be so kind. What can be done? He won't listen until he feels the pain. I must be blunt with him. Here he comes back from hunting. Oh dear, oh dear!
Good even, Varro. What! You come for money?
Good evening, Varro. What, have you come for money?
It is: and yours too, Isidore?
It is. And yours too, Isidore?
I wish we were all paid off!
So soon as dinner's done, we'll forth again. / My Alcibiades. With me? what is your will?
As soon as dinner's over, we'll go out again, my Alcibiades. Do you want me? What do you want?
My lord, here is a note of certain dues.
My lord, here's a list of certain debts.
From here in Athens, my lord.

Please it your lordship, he hath put me off / To the succession of new days this month: / My master is awak'd by great occasion / To call upon his own; and humbly prays you / That with your other noble parts you'll suit / In giving him his right.

If it please your lordship, he has put me off from day to day all this month. My master is pressed by great need to call in what's his, and humbly begs you to pay him what he's owed, as befits your other noble qualities.
Mine honest friend, / I prithee, but repair to me next morning.
My honest friend, please just come back to me tomorrow morning.
One Varro's servant, my good lord,—
I'm Varro's servant, my good lord...
From Isidore; he humbly prays your speedy payment.
I'm from Isidore. He humbly asks you for quick payment.
If you did know, my lord, my master's wants,—
If you knew, my lord, how much my master needs it...
'Twas due on forfeiture, my lord, six weeks and past.
It was due on penalty, my lord, more than six weeks ago.
Your steward puts me off, my lord; and / I am sent expressly to your lordship.
Your steward keeps putting me off, my lord, and I have been sent directly to your lordship.
Give me breath. / I do beseech you, good my lords, keep on; / I'll wait upon you instantly.
Give me room to breathe. Please, my good lords, go on ahead. I'll join you in a moment.
Come hither: pray you, / How goes the world, that I am thus encounter'd / With clamorous demands of date-broke bonds, / And the detention of long-since-due debts, / Against my honour?
Come here. Please tell me, what's going on, that I'm attacked like this with noisy demands for bonds past their date and debts long overdue, to the harm of my honour?
Please you, gentlemen, / The time is unagreeable to this business: / Your importunacy cease till after dinner, / That I may make his lordship understand / Wherefore you are not paid.
If you please, gentlemen, this isn't a good time for this business. Stop pressing until after dinner, so that I can explain to his lordship why you haven't been paid.
Do so, my friends. / See them well entertain'd.
Do that, my friends. (To Flavius) See that they're well looked after.
Stay, stay; here comes the fool with Apemantus: / Let's ha' some sport with 'em.
Wait, wait. Here comes the Fool with Apemantus. Let's have some fun with them.
A plague on him, the dog!
Are you talking to your own shadow?
No; 'tis to thyself. [To the FOOL] / Come away.
No, you're speaking to yourself. (To the Fool) Come on.
[To VARRO'S SERVANT] There's the fool hangs on your back already.
(To Varro's Servant) There, the fool is hanging on your back already.
No, thou stand'st single; thou'rt not on him yet.
No, you're standing alone. You haven't climbed onto him yet.
He last asked the question. Poor rogues and usurers' / men! bawds between gold and want!
The last one who asked a question. Poor rogues and moneylenders' servants! Pimps between gold and need!
That you ask me what you are, and do not know yourselves. Speak / to 'em, fool.
Because you ask me what you are, and don't know yourselves. Talk to them, fool.
Gramercies, good fool. How does your mistress?
Thank you, good fool. How's your mistress?
She's e'en setting on water to scald such chickens as you / are. Would we could see you at Corinth!
She's just putting water on to boil, to scald chickens like you. I wish we could see you at Corinth!
Look you, here comes my mistress' page.
Look, here comes my mistress's page.
[To the FOOL] Why, how now, Captain! what do you in this wise company? How dost / thou, Apemantus?
(To the Fool) Well, hello, captain! What are you doing in this wise company? How are you, Apemantus?
Would I had a rod in my mouth, that I might answer thee / profitably.
I wish I had a cane in my mouth, so I could give you a useful answer.
Prithee, Apemantus, read me the superscription of these / letters: I know not which is which.
Please, Apemantus, read me the addresses on these letters. I don't know which is which.
There will little learning die, then, that day thou art / hanged. This is to Lord Timon; this to Alcibiades. Go; thou wast / born a bastard, and thou'lt die a bawd.
Then there won't be much learning lost on the day you're hanged. This one is to Lord Timon, this one to Alcibiades. Go. You were born a bastard, and you'll die a pimp.
Thou wast whelped a dog, and thou shalt famish a dog's death. / Answer not; I am gone.
You were born a puppy, and you'll starve to death like a dog. Don't answer. I've gone.
E'en so thou outrunn'st grace.— / Fool, I will go with you to Lord Timon's.
In just the same way you run away from grace. Fool, I'll go with you to Lord Timon's.
If Timon stay at home. You three serve three usurers?
If Timon stays at home. You three serve three moneylenders?
Yes. We wish they served us!
So would I, as good a trick as ever hangman served thief.
So do I, the same way the hangman serves a thief.

I think no usurer but has a fool to his servant: my mistress / is one, and I am her fool. When men come to borrow of your / masters, they approach sadly, and go away merry; but they enter / my mistress' house merrily, and go away sadly: the reason of / this?

I think every moneylender has a fool as his servant. My mistress is one, and I'm her fool. When men come to borrow from your masters, they arrive sad and go away happy. But they come into my mistress's house happy and go away sad. What's the reason for that?
Do it, then, that we may account thee a whoremaster and a / knave; which notwithstanding, thou shalt be no less esteemed.
Do it, then, so we can count you a whoremonger and a rogue. Even so, you won't be thought any less of.

A fool in good clothes, and something like thee. 'Tis a / spirit: sometime 't appears like a lord; sometime like a lawyer; / sometime like a philosopher, with two stones more than's / artificial one. He is very often like a knight; and generally, / in all shapes that man goes up and down in from fourscore to / thirteen, this spirit walks in.

A fool in good clothes, something like you. It's a spirit. Sometimes it looks like a lord, sometimes like a lawyer, sometimes like a philosopher with two stones besides his philosopher's stone. Very often it looks like a knight. In general, this spirit walks around in every shape that men take, from eighty to thirteen.
Thou art not altogether a fool.
Nor thou altogether a wise man: / as much foolery as I have, so much wit thou lackest.
And you're not entirely a wise man. Whatever foolery I have, you lack that much sense.
That answer might have become Apemantus.
That answer might have come from Apemantus.
Aside, aside; here comes Lord Timon.
Step aside, step aside. Here comes Lord Timon.
I do not always follow lover, elder brother, and woman; / sometime the philosopher.
I don't always follow a lover, an elder brother and a woman. Sometimes I follow the philosopher.
Pray you walk near: I'll speak with you anon.
Please wait nearby. I'll speak to you soon.
You make me marvel: wherefore, ere this time, / Had you not fully laid my state before me, / That I might so have rated my expense / As I had leave of means?
You amaze me. Why didn't you set out my financial position fully before now, so that I could have matched my spending to what I could afford?
You would not hear me, / At many leisures I propos'd.
You wouldn't listen to me, at many free moments when I tried.
Go to: / Perchance some single vantages you took, / When my indisposition put you back; / And that unaptness made your minister / Thus to excuse yourself.
Come on. Perhaps you seized on a few odd moments when I wasn't in the mood and turned you away, and now you use that unwillingness to excuse yourself.

O my good lord! / At many times I brought in my accounts, / Laid them before you; you would throw them off, / And say you found them in mine honesty. / When for some trifling present you have bid me / Return so much, I have shook my head, and wept; / Yea, 'gainst the authority of manners, pray'd you / To hold your hand more close: I did endure / Not seldom, nor no slight checks, when I have / Prompted you in the ebb of your estate / And your great flow of debts. My loved lord, / Though you hear now, too late, yet now's a time, / The greatest of your having lacks a half / To pay your present debts.

Oh, my good lord! Many times I brought in my accounts and laid them in front of you. You would push them away and say you trusted my honesty. When you ordered me to give back a large sum in return for some trivial gift, I shook my head and wept. Yes, against all proper manners, I begged you to keep a tighter hold on your money. I often had to put up with harsh rebukes when I reminded you of your shrinking fortune and your swelling debts. My dear lord, though you're listening now, too late, now is the time to hear it: the whole of what you own is not enough to pay half your present debts.
Let all my land be sold.

'Tis all engag'd, some forfeited and gone; / And what remains will hardly stop the mouth / Of present dues; the future comes apace: / What shall defend the interim? and at length / How goes our reckoning?

It's all mortgaged, some of it forfeited and gone, and what's left will hardly stop the mouths of the debts already due. Future payments are coming fast. What will see us through until then? And in the end, how will our accounts stand?
To Lacedaemon did my land extend.
My lands stretched as far as Sparta.
O my good lord! the world is but a word; / Were it all yours to give it in a breath, / How quickly were it gone!
Oh, my good lord, the world is only a word. If it were all yours, and you could give it away in one breath, how quickly it would be gone!

If you suspect my husbandry or falsehood, / Call me before the exactest auditors / And set me on the proof. So the gods bless me, / When all our offices have been oppress'd / With riotous feeders, when our vaults have wept / With drunken spilth of wine, when every room / Hath blaz'd with lights and bray'd with minstrelsy, / I have retir'd me to a wasteful cock, / And set mine eyes at flow.

If you suspect my management or my honesty, call me before the strictest auditors and make me prove myself. As the gods bless me, when all our kitchens and pantries were crammed with greedy guests, when our cellars wept with spilled drunken wine, when every room blazed with lights and roared with music, I went off alone to a running tap and let my own tears run too.

Heavens! have I said, the bounty of this lord! / How many prodigal bits have slaves and peasants / This night englutted! Who is not Timon's? / What heart, head, sword, force, means, but is Lord Timon's? / Great Timon, noble, worthy, royal Timon!' / Ah! when the means are gone that buy this praise, / The breath is gone whereof this praise is made: / Feast-won, fast-lost; one cloud of winter showers, / These flies are couch'd.

"Heavens," people said, "how generous this lord is! How many lavish mouthfuls have slaves and peasants gobbled up tonight! Who doesn't belong to Timon? What heart, head, sword, strength or wealth isn't Lord Timon's? Great Timon, noble, worthy, royal Timon!" Ah, when the money that buys this praise is gone, the breath that makes the praise is gone too. Won by a feast, lost by a fast. One cloud of winter showers and these flies hide away.

Come, sermon me no further; / No villainous bounty yet hath pass'd my heart; / Unwisely, not ignobly, have I given. / Why dost thou weep? Canst thou the conscience lack, / To think I shall lack friends? Secure thy heart; / If I would broach the vessels of my love, / And try the argument of hearts by borrowing, / Men and men's fortunes could I frankly use / As I can bid thee speak.

Come, don't preach at me any more. My heart has never yet given anything for a wicked purpose. I have given unwisely, but not shamefully. Why are you crying? Do you really have so little faith as to think I'll lack friends? Set your heart at rest. If I open the casks of my friends' love and test their hearts by borrowing, I could use men and their fortunes as freely as I can tell you to speak.

And, in some sort, these wants of mine are crown'd / That I account them blessings; for by these / Shall I try friends. You shall perceive how you / Mistake my fortunes; I am wealthy in my friends. / Within there! Flaminius! Servilius!

And in a way these needs of mine are a crown, because I count them as blessings. By them I'll test my friends. You'll see how wrong you are about my fortune. I'm rich in my friends. Hey, in there! Flaminius! Servilius!

I will dispatch you severally: you to Lord Lucius; to Lord / Lucullus you: I hunted with his honour to-day; you, to / Sempronius. Commend me to their loves; and I am proud, say, that / my occasions have found time to use them toward a supply of / money: let the request be fifty talents.

I'll send you each on a separate errand. You go to Lord Lucius. You to Lord Lucullus; I went hunting with his honour today. You go to Sempronius. Give them my love, and say that I'm proud that my needs have given me a chance to use them for a loan of money. Ask for fifty talents.
As you have said, my lord.
[To another Servant] Go you, sir, to the senators,— / Of whom, even to the state's best health, I have / Deserv'd this hearing,—Bid 'em send o' the instant / A thousand talents to me.
(To another Servant) You, sir, go to the senators, whom I have served well enough, even for the good of the state, to deserve a hearing. Tell them to send me a thousand talents at once.
I have been bold,— / For that I knew it the most general way,— / To them to use your signet and your name; / But they do shake their heads, and I am here / No richer in return.
I was bold enough, since I knew it was the usual way, to use your seal and your name with them already. But they shook their heads, and I came back no richer.
Is that true? Can it be?

They answer, in a joint and corporate voice, / That now they are at fall, want treasure, cannot / Do what they would; are sorry; you are honourable; / But yet they could have wish'd; they know not; / Something hath been amiss; a noble nature / May catch a wrench; would all were well; 'tis pity; / And so, intending other serious matters, / After distasteful looks, and these hard fractions, / With certain half-caps and cold-moving nods, / They froze me into silence.

They reply, all together in one voice, that just now they're at a low point, short of money, can't do what they would like; they're sorry; you're honourable; but still they could have wished; they don't know; something has gone wrong; a noble nature can slip; they wish all were well; it's a pity. And so, pretending to have other important business, with sour looks and these broken-off phrases, with half-lifted hats and cold nods, they froze me into silence.

You gods, reward them! / Prithee, man, look cheerly. These old fellows / Have their ingratitude in them hereditary; / Their blood is cak'd, 'tis cold, it seldom flows; / 'Tis lack of kindly warmth they are not kind; / And nature, as it grows again toward earth, / Is fashion'd for the journey, dull and heavy. / [To a Servant] Go to Ventidius.—[To Flavius] / Prithee, be not sad, / Thou art true and honest; ingenuously I speak, / No blame belongs to thee.—[To Servant] Ventidius lately / Buried his father; by whose death he's stepp'd / Into a great estate. When he was poor, / Imprison'd and in scarcity of friends, / I clear'd him with five talents; greet him from me, / Bid him suppose some good necessity / Touches his friend, which craves to be remember'd / With those five talents.

May the gods repay them! Please, man, cheer up. These old men have ingratitude in their blood by inheritance. Their blood is clotted and cold; it hardly flows. They aren't kind because they lack natural warmth. And human nature, as it grows back towards the earth, becomes dull and heavy for the journey to the grave. (To a Servant) Go to Ventidius. (To Flavius) Please, don't be sad. You're loyal and honest. I say it frankly: you're not to blame. (To the Servant) Ventidius has just buried his father, and by his death he has come into a great fortune. When he was poor, in prison and short of friends, I freed him with five talents. Greet him for me. Tell him to imagine that some real need has touched his friend, which asks to be remembered with those five talents.
That had, give't these fellows / To whom 'tis instant due. Ne'er speak, or think / That Timon's fortunes 'mong his friends can sink.
(To Flavius) When you have it, give it to these men who must be paid at once. Never say or think that Timon's fortune can sink while he is among his friends.
I would I could not think it: / That thought is bounty's foe; / Being free itself, it thinks all others so.
I wish I couldn't think it. That thought is the enemy of generosity. Being generous itself, it thinks everyone else is too.
I have told my lord of you; he is coming down to you.
I've told my lord about you. He's coming down to see you.

[Aside] One of Lord Timon's men! a gift, I warrant. Why, this / hits right; I dreamt of a silver basin and ewer to-night. / Flaminius, honest Flaminius, you are very respectively / welcome, sir. Fill me some wine.

(Aside) One of Lord Timon's men! A present, I bet. Why, this fits nicely: I dreamed of a silver basin and jug last night. (To Flaminius) Flaminius, honest Flaminius, you're most respectfully welcome, sir. (To the Servant) Pour me some wine.
And how does that honourable, complete, freehearted / gentleman of Athens, thy very bountiful good lord and master?
And how is that honourable, perfect, generous gentleman of Athens, your very bountiful good lord and master?
I am right glad that his health is well, sir. And what / hast thou there under thy cloak, pretty Flaminius?
I'm very glad he's in good health, sir. And what have you got there under your cloak, pretty Flaminius?

Faith, nothing but an empty box, sir; which in my lord's / behalf, I come to entreat your honour to supply; who, having / great and instant occasion to use fifty talents, hath sent to / your lordship to furnish him, nothing doubting your present / assistance therein.

Honestly, nothing but an empty box, sir, which I've come on my lord's behalf to beg your honour to fill. He has a great and urgent need for fifty talents and has sent to your lordship to supply him, not doubting your immediate help.

La, la, la, la! 'Nothing doubting,' says he? Alas, good / lord! a noble gentleman 'tis, if he would not keep so good a / house. Many a time and often I ha' dined with him, and told him / on't; and come again to supper to him, of purpose to have him / spend less; and yet he would embrace no counsel, take no warning / by my coming. Every man has his fault, and honesty is his. I ha' / told him on't, but I could ne'er get him from it.

La, la, la, la! "Not doubting," he says? Oh dear, good lord! He's a noble gentleman, if only he didn't keep such an extravagant house. Time and again I've dined with him and told him so, and come back to supper with him on purpose to get him to spend less. But he wouldn't take any advice or any warning from my visits. Every man has his fault, and his is honesty. I've told him so, but I could never get him to change.
Please your lordship, here is the wine.
If it please your lordship, here's the wine.
Flaminius, I have noted thee always wise. Here's to thee.
Flaminius, I've always found you sensible. Here's to you.
Your lordship is pleased to say so.

I have observed thee always for a towardly prompt spirit, / give thee thy due, and one that knows what belongs to reason, and / canst use the time well, if the time use thee well: good parts in / thee. [To SERVANT]—Get you gone, sirrah.—

I've always seen you as a willing, quick-witted fellow, to give you your due, and one who knows what is reasonable and can make good use of an opportunity, if the opportunity treats you well. You have good qualities. (To the Servant) Off you go, fellow.

Draw nearer, honest Flaminius. Thy lord's a bountiful gentleman; / but thou art wise, and thou know'st well enough, although thou / comest to me, that this is no time to lend money, especially upon / bare friendship without security. Here's three solidares for / thee: good boy, wink at me, and say thou sawest me not. Fare thee / well.

Come closer, honest Flaminius. Your lord is a generous gentleman, but you're sensible, and you know well enough, even though you've come to me, that this is no time to lend money, especially on mere friendship without any security. Here are three coins for you. Good boy, turn a blind eye and say you didn't see me. Goodbye.
Is't possible the world should so much differ, / And we alive that liv'd? Fly, damned baseness, / To him that worships thee.
Is it possible that the world can change so much while we who lived in it are still alive? Fly, damned meanness, back to the man who worships you!
Ha! now I see thou art a fool, and fit for thy master.
Ha! Now I see you're a fool, a fit servant for your master.

May these add to the number that may scald thee! / Let molten coin be thy damnation, / Thou disease of a friend, and not himself! / Has friendship such a faint and milky heart / It turns in less than two nights? O you gods! / I feel my master's passion! This slave unto his honour / Has my lord's meat in him: / Why should it thrive and turn to nutriment / When he is turn'd to poison? / O! may diseases only work upon't! / And when he's sick to death, let not that part of nature / Which my lord paid for, be of any power / To expel sickness, but prolong his hour.

May these coins be among those that boil you in hell! May molten money be your damnation, you sickness pretending to be a friend! Has friendship such a weak and milky heart that it turns sour in less than two nights? Oh you gods! I feel my master's anger. This slave to his own rank still has my lord's food inside him. Why should it do him good and nourish him, when he himself has turned to poison? Oh, may it only feed diseases! And when he's sick to death, may the part of his body that my lord paid for have no power to drive out the sickness, but only drag out his dying.
Who, the Lord Timon? he is my very good friend, and an / honourable gentleman.
Who, Lord Timon? He's a very good friend of mine and an honourable gentleman.

We know him for no less, though we are but strangers to him. But / I can tell you one thing, my lord, and which I hear from common / rumours: now Lord Timon's happy hours are done and past, and his / estate shrinks from him.
We know he is, though we're only strangers to him. But I can tell you one thing, my lord, which I hear from common gossip: Lord Timon's happy times are over, and his fortune is shrinking away.
Fie, no, do not believe it; he cannot want for money.
Nonsense, don't believe it. He can't be short of money.

But believe you this, my lord, that, not long ago, one of his men / was with the Lord Lucullus to borrow so many talents, nay, urged / extremely for't, and showed what necessity belonged to't, and yet / was denied.

But believe this, my lord: not long ago one of his men went to Lord Lucullus to borrow a number of talents, and pressed him hard for them, and explained how badly they were needed, and still he was refused.
I tell you, denied, my lord.
I tell you, refused, my lord.

What a strange case was that! now, before the gods, I am / ashamed on't. Denied that honourable man! there was very little / honour showed in't. For my own part, I must needs confess, I have / received some small kindnesses from him, as money, plate, jewels, / and such like trifles, nothing comparing to his; yet, had he / mistook him, and sent to me, I should ne'er have denied his / occasion so many talents.

What a strange thing! Now, by the gods, I'm ashamed of it. To refuse that honourable man! There was very little honour shown in that. For my own part, I must admit I've received a few small kindnesses from him, like money, silver, jewels and trifles of that sort, nothing compared with what Lucullus got. Still, if he had passed over Lucullus and sent to me, I would never have refused him so many talents in his need.
See, by good hap, yonder's my lord; I have sweat to see / his honour. [To LUCIUS] My honoured lord!
Look, by good luck there's my lord. I've sweated to find his honour. (To Lucius) My honoured lord!
Servilius! you are kindly met, sir. Fare thee well: commend / me to thy honourable virtuous lord, my very exquisite friend.
Servilius! Good to see you, sir. Goodbye. Give my regards to your honourable, virtuous lord, my most excellent friend.
May it please your honour, my lord hath sent—
If it please your honour, my lord has sent...
Ha! What has he sent? I am so much endeared to that lord; / he's ever sending: how shall I thank him, thinkest thou? And what / has he sent now?
Ha! What has he sent? I'm so much in that lord's debt; he's always sending me things. How do you think I can thank him? And what has he sent now?
Has only sent his present occasion now, my lord; / requesting your lordship to supply his instant use with so many / talents.
He has only sent you his present need, my lord, asking your lordship to supply him at once with a number of talents.
I know his lordship is but merry with me; / He cannot want fifty-five hundred talents.
I know his lordship is only joking with me. He can't be short of fifty-five hundred talents.
But in the mean time he wants less, my lord. / If his occasion were not virtuous, / I should not urge it half so faithfully.
But just now he needs much less, my lord. If his need weren't an honest one, I wouldn't press it half so earnestly.
On my soul, it's true, sir.

What a wicked beast was I to disfurnish myself against such / a good time, when I might ha' shown myself honourable! how / unluckily it happened, that I should purchase the day before for / a little part, and undo a great deal of honour! Servilius, now, / before the gods, I am not able to do; the more beast, I say; I / was sending to use Lord Timon myself, these gentlemen can / witness; but I would not, for the wealth of Athens, I had done it / now. Commend me bountifully to his good lordship; and I hope his / honour will conceive the fairest of me, because I have no power / to be kin: and tell him this from me, I count it one of my / greatest afflictions say, that I cannot pleasure such an / honourable gentleman. Good Servilius, will you befriend me so far / as to use mine own words to him?

What a wicked beast I was to leave myself without money just when I could have shown myself honourable! How unlucky that only the day before I made a purchase that brought me a little profit and lost me a great deal of honour! Servilius, now, by the gods, I'm not able to do it. All the more beast me, I say! I was about to send to Lord Timon to borrow from him myself, as these gentlemen can witness. But I wouldn't have done it now for all the wealth of Athens. Give my warmest regards to his good lordship. I hope his honour will think the best of me, since I have no power to be kind. And tell him this from me: say I count it one of my greatest sorrows that I can't oblige such an honourable gentleman. Good Servilius, will you do me the favour of telling him in my own words?
I'll look you out a good turn, Servilius.
I'll find a good turn to do for you, Servilius.
True, as you said, Timon is shrunk indeed; / And he that's once denied will hardly speed.
It's true, as you said: Timon really has come down in the world. And a man who has been refused once will hardly succeed elsewhere.

Why, this is the world's soul; and just of the same piece / Is every flatterer's spirit. Who can call him / His friend that dips in the same dish? for, in / My knowing, Timon has been this lord's father, / And kept his credit with his purse, / Supported his estate; nay, Timon's money / Has paid his men their wages: He ne'er drinks / But Timon's silver treads upon his lip; / And yet, O! see the monstrousness of man, / When he looks out in an ungrateful shape, / He does deny him, in respect of his, / What charitable men afford to beggars.

Why, this is the spirit of the world, and every flatterer's spirit is cut from the same cloth. Who can call a man who eats from the same dish his friend? As far as I know, Timon has been a father to this lord. He kept up his credit with his own purse and supported his estate. Yes, Timon's money has paid his servants' wages. He never drinks without Timon's silver touching his lips. And yet, oh, see how monstrous man is when he shows his ungrateful side! Compared with what he has, he refuses Timon what charitable men give to beggars.

For mine own part, / I never tasted Timon in my life, / Nor came any of his bounties over me / To mark me for his friend; yet I protest, / For his right noble mind, illustrious virtue, / And honourable carriage, / Had his necessity made use of me, / I would have put my wealth into donation, / And the best half should have return'd to him, / So much I love his heart. But, I perceive, / Men must learn now with pity to dispense; / For policy sits above conscience.

For my own part, I've never enjoyed anything of Timon's in my life. None of his gifts ever came my way to make me his friend. Yet I swear, for his truly noble mind, his shining virtue and his honourable behaviour, if his need had turned to me, I would have treated my wealth as a gift and given the better half back to him, I love his heart so much. But I see that men must now learn to do without pity, because self-interest now ranks above conscience.

Must he needs trouble me in't? Hum! 'bove all others? / He might have tried Lord Lucius, or Lucullus; / And now Ventidius is wealthy too, / Whom he redeem'd from prison: all these / Owe their estates unto him.

Must he trouble me with this? Hmm! Me before everyone else? He might have tried Lord Lucius, or Lucullus. And now Ventidius is rich too, whom he bought out of prison. All of these owe their fortunes to him.
My lord, / They have all been touch'd and found base metal, for / They have all denied him.
My lord, they have all been tested like coins and found to be base metal, because they have all refused him.

How! have they denied him? / Has Ventidius and Lucullus denied him? / And does he send to me? Three? Hum! / It shows but little love or judgment in him: / Must I be his last refuge? His friends, like physicians, / Thrice give him over; must I take the cure upon me? / Has much disgrac'd me in't; I'm angry at him, / That might have known my place. I see no sense for't, / But his occasions might have woo'd me first; / For, in my conscience, I was the first man / That e'er received gift from him: / And does he think so backwardly of me now, / That I'll requite it last? No: / So it may prove an argument of laughter / To the rest, and I 'mongst lords be thought a fool. / I had rather than the worth of thrice the sum, / Had sent to me first, but for my mind's sake; / I'd such a courage to do him good. But now return, / And with their faint reply this answer join; / Who bates mine honour shall not know my coin.

What! Have they refused him? Have Ventidius and Lucullus refused him? And now he sends to me? Three of them? Hmm! It shows very little love or judgement in him. Must I be his last resort? His friends, like doctors, have given him up three times over. Must I take on the cure? He has insulted me badly by this. I'm angry with him; he should have known my rank. I can see no reason why his needs shouldn't have come to me first, because, honestly, I was the first man who ever received a gift from him. And does he think so little of me now that I'll be the last to repay it? No. That would make me a laughing stock among the others, and I'd be thought a fool among lords. I'd rather he had sent to me first, just for my own sake, than be given three times the sum, I was so eager to help him. But now go back, and add this answer to their feeble replies: whoever lowers my honour won't see my money.

Excellent! Your lordship's a goodly villain. The devil / knew not what he did when he made man politic; he crossed / himself by't: and I cannot think but, in the end the villainies / of man will set him clear. How fairly this lord strives to appear / foul! takes virtuous copies to be wicked, like those that under / hot ardent zeal would set whole realms on fire: / Of such a nature is his politic love. / This was my lord's best hope; now all are fled / Save only the gods. Now his friends are dead, / Doors, that were ne'er acquainted with their wards / Many a bounteous year, must be employ'd / Now to guard sure their master: / And this is all a liberal course allows: / Who cannot keep his wealth must keep his house.

Excellent! Your lordship is a fine villain. The devil didn't know what he was doing when he made man crafty; he got in his own way by it. I can't help thinking that in the end man's villainy will make the devil look innocent. How cleverly this lord tries to look foul! He uses virtuous examples to be wicked, like those who, under a show of burning religious zeal, would set whole kingdoms on fire. His crafty love is of that kind. He was my lord's best hope. Now everyone has run away except the gods. Now that his friends are dead, doors that never knew their bolts for many generous years must be used to guard their master safely. This is all that a generous life leaves him: a man who can't keep his wealth must keep to his house to avoid arrest.
Well met; good morrow, Titus and Hortensius.
Well met. Good morning, Titus and Hortensius.
The like to you, kind Varro.
The same to you, kind Varro.
