Lucius! What! do we meet together!
Lucius! What, are we all meeting here?
Ay, and I think one business does command us all; for mine is / money.
Yes, and I think one errand brings us all, because mine is money.
Welcome, good brother. / What do you think the hour?
Welcome, good brother. What time do you think it is?
Is not my lord seen yet?
Hasn't my lord been seen yet?
I wonder on't; he was wont to shine at seven.
I'm surprised. He used to shine out at seven.

Ay, but the days are waxed shorter with him: / You must consider that a prodigal course / Is like the sun's, but not, like his, recoverable. / I fear, / 'Tis deepest winter in Lord Timon's purse; / That is, one may reach deep enough, and yet / Find little.

Yes, but his days have grown shorter. You must remember that a spendthrift's course is like the sun's, but, unlike the sun's, it can't come round again. I'm afraid it's deepest winter in Lord Timon's purse. That is, you can reach deep into it and still find little.
I am of your fear for that.
I share your fear on that.
I'll show you how to observe a strange event. / Your lord sends now for money.
I'll show you something strange. Your lord is now sending to Timon for money.
And he wears jewels now of Timon's gift, / For which I wait for money.
And he's wearing jewels that Timon gave him, which I'm waiting to be paid for.
Mark, how strange it shows, / Timon in this should pay more than he owes: / And e'en as if your lord should wear rich jewels, / And send for money for 'em.
Look how strange it seems: in this way Timon will pay more than he owes. It's just as if your lord should wear rich jewels and send to Timon for money to pay for them.
I'm weary of this charge, the gods can witness: / I know my lord hath spent of Timon's wealth, / And now ingratitude makes it worse than stealth.
I'm sick of this errand, as the gods are my witness. I know my lord has spent Timon's wealth, and now his ingratitude makes it worse than theft.
Yes, mine's three thousand crowns; what's yours?
Yes, mine is three thousand crowns. What's yours?
'Tis much deep: and it should seem by the sum, / Your master's confidence was above mine; / Else, surely, his had equall'd.
That's a lot. And it seems from the size of the sum that your master trusted Timon more than mine did. Otherwise, surely, his loan would have been as big.
Flaminius! Sir, a word. Pray, is my lord ready to / come forth?
Flaminius! Sir, a word. Please, is my lord ready to come out?
We attend his lordship; pray, signify so much.
We're waiting for his lordship. Please tell him so.
I need not tell him that; he knows you are too diligent.
I don't need to tell him that. He knows you are all too eager.
Ha! is not that his steward muffled so? / He goes away in a cloud: call him, call him.
Ha! Isn't that his steward, wrapped up like that? He's slipping away in a cloud. Call him, call him.
What do you ask of me, my friend?
What do you want from me, my friend?
We wait for certain money here, sir.
We're waiting here for some money that's certain, sir.

Ay, / If money were as certain as your waiting, / 'Twere sure enough. / Why then preferr'd you not your sums and bills, / When your false masters eat of my lord's meat? / Then they could smile and fawn upon his debts, / And take down the interest into their gluttonous maws. / You do yourselves but wrong to stir me up; / Let me pass quietly: / Believe't, my lord and I have made an end; / I have no more to reckon, he to spend.

Yes. If money were as certain as your waiting, it would be sure enough. Why didn't you hand in your sums and bills when your false masters were eating my lord's food? Then they could smile and fawn on his debts and swallow the interest into their greedy stomachs. You only harm yourselves by provoking me. Let me pass in peace. Believe me, my lord and I have finished: I have no more to count, and he has no more to spend.
Ay, but this answer will not serve.
Yes, but that answer won't serve.
If 'twill not serve, 'tis not so base as you; / For you serve knaves.
If it won't serve, it's not as low as you, because you serve rogues.
How! what does his cashiered worship mutter?
What! What is his dismissed worship muttering?
No matter what; he's poor, and that's revenge enough. Who can / speak broader than he that has no house to put his head in? such / may rail against great buildings.
Never mind what. He's poor, and that's revenge enough. Who can speak more freely than a man who has no house to shelter in? Men like that can rail against great buildings.
O, here's Servilius; now we shall know some answer.
Oh, here's Servilius. Now we'll get some answer.

If I might beseech you, gentlemen, to repair some other / hour, I should derive much from't; for, take't of my soul, my / lord leans wondrously to discontent. His comfortable temper has / forsook him; he's much out of health, and keeps his chamber.

If I might beg you, gentlemen, to come back at some other time, I'd be most grateful. For, believe me on my soul, my lord is terribly inclined to gloom. His cheerful temper has deserted him. He's very unwell and keeps to his room.
Many do keep their chambers are not sick: / And, if it be so far beyond his health, / Methinks he should the sooner pay his debts, / And make a clear way to the gods.
Plenty of people keep to their rooms who aren't sick. And if he's as ill as that, I think he should pay his debts all the sooner and clear his way to the gods.
We cannot take this for answer, sir.
We can't accept this as an answer, sir.
[Within] Servilius, help! my lord! my lord!
(Offstage) Servilius, help! My lord! My lord!

What! are my doors oppos'd against my passage? / Have I been ever free, and must my house / Be my retentive enemy, my gaol? / The place which I have feasted, does it now, / Like all mankind, show me an iron heart?

What! Are my own doors barred against me? Have I always been free, and must my house now be my enemy that holds me in, my prison? Does the place where I have feasted others now show me an iron heart, like all mankind?
My lord, here is my bill.
Knock me down with 'em: cleave me to the girdle.
Knock me down with them. Split me in two to the waist.
Five thousand drops pays that. What yours? and yours?
Five thousand drops will pay that. What's yours? And yours?
Tear me, take me; and the gods fall upon you!
Tear me apart, take me, and may the gods fall on you!
Faith, I perceive our masters may throw their caps at their / money: these debts may well be called desperate ones, for a / madman owes 'em.
Honestly, I think our masters can say goodbye to their money. These debts can rightly be called desperate ones, because a madman owes them.
They have e'en put my breath from me, the slaves. / Creditors? devils!
The slaves have almost knocked the breath out of me. Creditors? Devils!
What if it should be so?
I'll have it so. My steward!
So fitly! Go, bid all my friends again: / Lucius, Lucullus, and Sempronius; all: / I'll once more feast the rascals.
Just in time! Go and invite all my friends again: Lucius, Lucullus and Sempronius, all of them. I'll feast the rascals once more.
O my lord! / You only speak from your distracted soul; / There is not so much left to furnish out / A moderate table.
Oh, my lord! You only speak like that because your mind is disturbed. There isn't enough left to set out a modest table.
Be it not in thy care: go. / I charge thee, invite them all: let in the tide / Of knaves once more; my cook and I'll provide.
Don't you worry about that. Go. I order you to invite them all. Let the tide of rogues in once more. My cook and I will provide.
My lord, you have my voice to it: the fault's / Bloody. 'tis necessary he should die; / Nothing emboldens sin so much as mercy.
My lord, you have my vote for it. The crime was bloody, and he must die. Nothing encourages sin so much as mercy.
Most true; the law shall bruise him.
Very true. The law shall crush him.
Honour, health, and compassion to the senate!
Honour, health and compassion to the Senate!

I am a humble suitor to your virtues; / For pity is the virtue of the law, / And none but tyrants use it cruelly. / It pleases time and fortune to lie heavy / Upon a friend of mine, who, in hot blood / Hath stepp'd into the law, which is past depth / To those that without heed do plunge into't. / He is a man, setting his fate aside, / Of comely virtues; / Nor did he soil the fact with cowardice,— / An honour in him which buys out his fault,— / But, with a noble fury and fair spirit, / Seeing his reputation touch'd to death, / He did oppose his foe; / And with such sober and unnoted passion / He did behave his anger, ere 'twas spent, / As if he had but prov'd an argument.

I come humbly to appeal to your virtues, because pity is the virtue of the law, and only tyrants use the law cruelly. Time and fortune have chosen to weigh heavily on a friend of mine who, in the heat of anger, has fallen foul of the law, which is too deep for anyone who plunges into it carelessly. Apart from this misfortune, he is a man of fine qualities. He did not stain the deed with cowardice, an honour that pays for his fault. With noble anger and a fair spirit, seeing his reputation wounded to the death, he stood up to his enemy. And he kept his anger so controlled and quiet, until it was spent, that it was as if he had only been arguing a point.

You undergo too strict a paradox, / Striving to make an ugly deed look fair: / Your words have took such pains as if they labour'd / To bring manslaughter into form, and set / Quarrelling upon the head of valour; which indeed / Is valour misbegot, and came into the world / When sects and factions were newly born. / He's truly valiant that can wisely suffer / The worst that man can breathe, and make his wrongs / his outsides, to wear them like his raiment, carelessly, / And ne'er prefer his injuries to his heart, / To bring it into danger. / If wrongs be evils, and enforce us kill, / What folly 'tis to hazard life for ill!

You are defending too strained a contradiction, trying to make an ugly deed look fair. Your words have worked so hard that it seems they are trying to make manslaughter respectable and to treat quarrelling as a form of courage. That kind of courage is a bastard, born into the world when parties and factions first began. The truly brave man is one who can wisely bear the worst insults men can speak, and treat his wrongs as outward things, wearing them carelessly like his clothes, never taking his injuries to heart and so putting it in danger. If wrongs are evils that force us to kill, what folly it is to risk our lives for evil!
You cannot make gross sins look clear; / To revenge is no valour, but to bear.
You can't make gross sins look innocent. Courage isn't taking revenge; it's enduring.

My lords, then, under favour, pardon me, / If I speak like a captain. / Why do fond men expose themselves to battle, / And not endure all threats? sleep upon't, / And let the foes quietly cut their throats / Without repugnancy? If there be / Such valour in the bearing, what make we / Abroad? why, then, women are more valiant / That stay at home, if bearing carry it, / And the ass more captain than the lion, the felon / Loaden with irons wiser than the judge, / If wisdom be in suffering. O my lords! / As you are great, be pitifully good: / Who cannot condemn rashness in cold blood? / To kill, I grant, is sin's extremest gust; / But, in defence, by mercy, 'tis most just. / To be in anger is impiety; / But who is man that is not angry? / Weigh but the crime with this.

Then, my lords, with your permission, forgive me if I speak like a soldier. Why do foolish men expose themselves in battle, instead of putting up with all threats, sleeping on them, and letting their enemies quietly cut their throats without resisting? If there is such courage in enduring, what are we doing fighting abroad? Then women who stay at home are braver, if enduring wins the prize, and the ass is a better captain than the lion, and the criminal loaded with chains is wiser than the judge, if wisdom lies in suffering. Oh my lords, since you are great, be good and merciful. Who can't condemn rashness when his own blood is cold? I grant that killing is the most extreme taste of sin, but when it is done in self-defence it is, in mercy, entirely just. Anger is ungodly, but what man is never angry? Just weigh the crime with that in mind.
In vain! his service done / At Lacedaemon and Byzantium / Were a sufficient briber for his life.
Wasting my breath! The service he did at Sparta and Byzantium should be enough to buy his life.
I say, my lords, has done fair service, / And slain in fight many of your enemies. / How full of valour did he bear himself / In the last conflict, and made plenteous wounds!
I say, my lords, he has served you well and killed many of your enemies in battle. How bravely he behaved in the last fight, and how many wounds he gave!

He has made too much plenty with 'em; / He's a sworn rioter; he has a sin that often / Drowns him and takes his valour prisoner; / If there were no foes, that were enough / To overcome him; in that beastly fury / He has been known to commit outrages / And cherish factions; 'tis inferr'd to us, / His days are foul and his drink dangerous.

He has made too many wounds. He's a hardened brawler. He has a sin that often drowns him and takes his courage prisoner. If there were no enemies, that alone would be enough to beat him. In that beastly drunken fury he has been known to commit outrages and stir up factions. We are told that his days are foul and his drinking dangerous.

Hard fate! he might have died in war. / My lords, if not for any parts in him,— / Though his right arm might purchase his own time, / And be in debt to none,—yet, more to move you, / Take my deserts to his, and join 'em both; / And, for I know your reverend ages love / Security, I'll pawn my victories, all / My honour to you, upon his good returns. / If by this crime he owes the law his life, / Why, let the war receive't in valiant gore; / For law is strict, and war is nothing more.

A cruel fate! He could have died in war. My lords, if not for any qualities of his own, though his right arm could buy him the rest of his life and owe nobody anything, then, to move you more, add my services to his and join them together. And because I know your reverend ages love security, I'll pledge all my victories and all my honour to you that he will repay you well. If he owes the law his life for this crime, let war take it in brave bloodshed, because war is just as strict as law.
We are for law; he dies: urge it no more, / On height of our displeasure. Friend or brother, / He forfeits his own blood that spills another.
We stand for the law. He dies. Don't press it any further, or face our greatest displeasure. Friend or brother, a man who spills another's blood loses his own.
Must it be so? it must not be. My lords, / I do beseech you, know me.
Must it be so? It must not. My lords, I beg you, remember who I am.
I cannot think but your age has forgot me; / It could not else be I should prove so base, / To sue, and be denied such common grace. / My wounds ache at you.
I can only think that your old age has forgotten me. Otherwise it couldn't be that I am treated so lowly as to beg and be refused such an ordinary favour. My wounds ache at the sight of you.
Do you dare our anger? / 'Tis in few words, but spacious in effect; / We banish thee for ever.
Do you dare provoke our anger? It's said in a few words, but its effect is wide: we banish you forever.
Banish me! / Banish your dotage; banish usury, / That makes the Senate ugly.
Banish me! Banish your senility. Banish moneylending, which makes the Senate ugly.
If, after two days' shine, Athens contain thee, / Attend our weightier judgment. And, not to swell our spirit, / He shall be executed presently.
If Athens still holds you after two days, expect a heavier sentence. And, so as not to inflame our anger further, your friend will be executed at once.

Now the gods keep you old enough; that you may live / Only in bone, that none may look on you! / I'm worse than mad: I have kept back their foes, / While they have told their money and let out / Their coin upon large interest; I myself / Rich only in large hurts: all those for this? / Is this the balsam that the usuring senate / Pours into captains' wounds? Banishment! / It comes not ill; I hate not to be banish'd; / It is a cause worthy my spleen and fury, / That I may strike at Athens. I'll cheer up / My discontented troops, and lay for hearts. / 'Tis honour with most lands to be at odds; / Soldiers should brook as little wrongs as gods.

Now may the gods keep you alive until you are old enough to be nothing but bones, so that no one can bear to look at you! I'm worse than mad. I've kept their enemies away while they counted their money and lent it out at high interest, and I myself am rich only in great wounds. All that for this? Is this the healing ointment that the moneylending Senate pours into soldiers' wounds? Banishment! It doesn't come badly. I don't mind being banished. It's a cause worthy of my rage and fury, so that I can strike at Athens. I'll cheer up my discontented troops and win their hearts. It's an honour to be at war with most countries. Soldiers should put up with wrongs as little as gods do.
The good time of day to you, sir.
I also wish it to you. I think this honourable lord / did but try us this other day.
The same to you. I think this honourable lord was only testing us the other day.
Upon that were my thoughts tiring when we encountered: / I hope it is not so low with him as he made it seem in the trial / of his several friends.
That's just what I was thinking about when we met. I hope he isn't as badly off as he made himself seem when he tested his various friends.
It should not be, by the persuasion of his new feasting.
He can't be, judging by this new feast.
I should think so: he hath sent me an earnest inviting, / which many my near occasions did urge me to put off; but he hath / conjured me beyond them, and I must needs appear.
I should think so. He sent me an urgent invitation, which many pressing affairs of mine made me want to refuse, but he begged me so hard that I had to come.
In like manner was I in debt to my importunate business, but he / would not hear my excuse. I am sorry, when he sent to borrow of / me, that my provision was out.
In the same way I had urgent business to attend to, but he wouldn't accept my excuse. I'm sorry that when he sent to borrow from me my money had run out.
I am sick of that grief too, as I understand how all things go.
I'm sick with the same regret, now that I understand how things are.
Every man here's so. What would he have borrowed you?
Everyone here is. How much did he want to borrow from you?
He sent to me, sir—here he comes.
He sent to me, sir... here he comes.
With all my heart, gentlemen both; And how fare you?
Welcome with all my heart, both of you, gentlemen. And how are you?
Ever at the best, hearing well of your lordship.
Always at our best when we hear your lordship is well.
The swallow follows not summer more willing than we / your lordship.
The swallow doesn't follow summer more willingly than we follow your lordship.

[Aside] Nor more willingly leaves winter; such summer-birds / are men. Gentlemen, our dinner will not recompense this long / stay: feast your ears with the music awhile, if they will fare so / harshly o' the trumpet's sound; we shall to't presently.

(Aside) Nor leave winter more willingly. Men are summer birds like that. (Aloud) Gentlemen, our dinner won't make up for this long wait. Feast your ears on the music for a while, if they can stand such a harsh diet as the trumpet's sound. We'll eat in a moment.
I hope it remains not unkindly with your lordship that / I return'd you an empty messenger.
I hope your lordship doesn't still hold it against me that I sent your messenger back empty-handed.
O! sir, let it not trouble you.
Oh, sir, don't let it trouble you.
Ah! my good friend, what cheer?
Ah, my good friend, how are you?
My most honourable lord, I am e'en sick of shame, that / when your lordship this other day sent to me I was so / unfortunate a beggar.
My most honourable lord, I'm sick with shame that when your lordship sent to me the other day I was so unluckily without money.
If you had sent but two hours before,—
If you had only sent two hours earlier...
Let it not cumber your better remembrance.
Don't let it burden your better memories.
Come, bring it all in together.
Doubt not that, if money and the season can yield it.
No doubt of that, if money and the season can provide it.
How do you? What's the news?
How are you? What's the news?
Alcibiades is banished: hear you of it?
Alcibiades has been banished. Have you heard?
It's true, you can be sure of it.
My worthy friends, will you draw near?
My worthy friends, will you come to the table?
I'll tell you more anon. Here's a noble feast toward.
I'll tell you more later. There's a fine feast coming.
This is the old man still.
He's the same old Timon still.
Will it last? Will it last?
It does; but time will—and so—
It does for now, but time will... and so...

Each man to his stool with that spur as he would to the lip / of his mistress; your diet shall be in all places alike. Make not / a city feast of it, to let the meat cool ere we can agree upon / the first place: sit, sit. The gods require our thanks.— / You great benefactors sprinkle our society with thankfulness. / For your own gifts make yourselves praised: but reserve still to / give, lest your deities be despised. Lend to each man enough, / that one need not lend to another; for, were your god-heads to / borrow of men, men would forsake the gods. Make the meat be / beloved more than the man that gives it. Let no assembly of / twenty be without a score of villains: if there sit twelve women / at the table, let a dozen of them be as they are. The rest of / your foes, O gods! the senators of Athens, together with the / common lag of people, what is amiss in them, you gods, make / suitable for destruction. For these my present friends, as they / are to me nothing, so in nothing bless them, and to nothing are / they welcome. / Uncover, dogs, and lap.

Every man go to his seat as eagerly as he would go to kiss his mistress. The food will be the same everywhere. Don't make a formal city banquet of it, letting the food go cold while we argue about who takes the top place. Sit, sit. The gods require our thanks. (Saying grace) You great benefactors, sprinkle our company with thankfulness. Make yourselves praised for your own gifts, but always keep something back to give, in case your godhead is despised. Lend each man enough so that no one need lend to another, because if you gods had to borrow from men, men would abandon the gods. Make the food more loved than the man who gives it. Let no gathering of twenty be without a score of villains. If twelve women sit at the table, let a dozen of them be what they are. As for the rest of your enemies, oh gods, the senators of Athens together with the common rabble, whatever is wrong in them, you gods, make it fit for destruction. As for my present friends here, since they are nothing to me, bless them with nothing, and to nothing they are welcome. Uncover the dishes, dogs, and lap it up.

May you a better feast never behold, / You knot of mouth-friends! smoke and lukewarm water / Is your perfection. This is Timon's last; / Who, stuck and spangled with your flatteries, / Washes it off, and sprinkles in your faces

May you never see a better feast, you gang of friends in words only! Steam and lukewarm water are your perfect likeness. This is Timon's last feast. Smeared and spangled with your flattery, he washes it off and sprinkles in your faces

Your reeking villainy. Live loath'd, and long, / Most smiling, smooth, detested parasites, / Courteous destroyers, affable wolves, meek bears, / You fools of fortune, trencher-friends, time's flies, / Cap and knee slaves, vapours, and minute-jacks! / Of man and beast the infinite malady / Crust you quite o'er! What, dost thou go? / Soft! take thy physic first,—thou too,—and thou;— / Stay, I will lend thee money, borrow none.

your stinking villainy. May you live hated, and live long, you smiling, smooth, loathed parasites, polite destroyers, friendly wolves, gentle bears, you fools of fortune, friends of the dinner plate, fair-weather flies, bowing and kneeling slaves, puffs of air, clockwork puppets! May every disease of man and beast cover you completely with scabs! What, are you going? Wait! Take your medicine first, and you too, and you. Stay, I'll lend you money, not borrow any.
What, all in motion? Henceforth be no feast, / Whereat a villain's not a welcome guest. / Burn, house! sink Athens! henceforth hated be / Of Timon man and all humanity!
What, all running away? From now on let there be no feast where a villain is not a welcome guest. Burn, house! Sink, Athens! From now on let man and all humanity be hated by Timon!
Know you the quality of Lord Timon's fury?
Do you understand what Lord Timon's fury is about?
Push! did you see my cap?
Bah! Have you seen my hat?
He's but a mad lord, and nought but humour sways him. / He gave me a jewel th' other day, and now he has beat it out of / my hat: did you see my jewel?
He's just a mad lord, ruled by nothing but his moods. He gave me a jewel the other day, and now he has knocked it out of my hat. Have you seen my jewel?
I can feel it in my bones.
One day he gives us diamonds, next day stones.
One day he gives us diamonds, the next day stones.

Let me look back upon thee. O thou wall, / That girdles in those wolves, dive in the earth, / And fence not Athens! Matrons, turn incontinent! / Obedience fail in children! slaves and fools, / Pluck the grave wrinkled senate from the bench, / And minister in their steads! To general filths / Convert, o' the instant, green virginity. / Do't in your parents' eyes! Bankrupts, hold fast; / Rather than render back, out with your knives, / And cut your trusters' throats. Bound servants, steal,— / Large-handed robbers your grave masters are, / And pill by law. Maid, to thy master's bed; / Thy mistress is o' the brothel! Son of sixteen, / Pluck the lin'd crutch from thy old limping sire, / With it beat out his brains! Piety, and fear, / Religion to the gods, peace, justice, truth, / Domestic awe, night-rest and neighbourhood, / Instruction, manners, mysteries and trades, / Degrees, observances, customs and laws, / Decline to your confounding contraries, / And let confusion live! Plagues incident to men, / Your potent and infectious fevers heap / On Athens, ripe for stroke! Thou cold sciatica, / Cripple our senators, that their limbs may halt / As lamely as their manners! Lust and liberty / Creep in the minds and marrows of our youth, / That 'gainst the stream of virtue they may strive, / And drown themselves in riot! Itches, blains, / Sow all the Athenian bosoms, and their crop / Be general leprosy! Breath infect breath, / That their society, as their friendship, may / Be merely poison! Nothing I'll bear from thee / But nakedness, thou detestable town! / Take thou that too, with multiplying bans! / Timon will to the woods; where he shall find / Th' unkindest beast more kinder than mankind. / The gods confound—hear me, you good gods all— / The Athenians both within and out that wall! / And grant, as Timon grows, his hate may grow / To the whole race of mankind, high and low! / Amen.

Let me look back at you. Oh you wall that circles those wolves, sink into the earth and stop protecting Athens! Wives, become unchaste! Children, stop obeying! Slaves and fools, drag the grave, wrinkled senators from their bench and rule in their place! Let young virgins turn at once into common whores; do it in front of your parents! Bankrupts, hold on to what you have; rather than pay it back, take out your knives and cut your creditors' throats! Bound servants, steal: your grave masters are big-handed robbers who plunder by law. Maid, go to your master's bed; your mistress is in the brothel! Son of sixteen, snatch the padded crutch from your old limping father and beat his brains out with it! Piety and fear, reverence for the gods, peace, justice, truth, respect within the home, night's rest and neighbourliness, teaching, manners, crafts and trades, ranks, ceremonies, customs and laws, collapse into your destructive opposites, and let chaos live! Plagues that afflict men, pile your powerful, infectious fevers on Athens, which is ripe to be struck down! Cold sciatica, cripple our senators, so that their limbs limp as lamely as their morals! Let lust and licence creep into the minds and bones of our young men, so that they swim against the stream of virtue and drown in debauchery! Itches and blisters, be sown in every Athenian breast, and let the harvest be leprosy for all! Let breath infect breath, so that their company, like their friendship, is nothing but poison! I'll take nothing from you but my nakedness, you hateful town! Take that too, with curses multiplied! Timon will go to the woods, where he'll find the cruellest beast kinder than mankind. May the gods destroy (hear me, all you good gods) the Athenians both inside and outside that wall! And grant that, as Timon grows older, his hatred may grow towards the whole human race, high and low! Amen.
Hear you, Master Steward! where's our master? / Are we undone? cast off? nothing remaining?
Listen, Master Steward! Where's our master? Are we ruined? Thrown out? Is nothing left?
Alack! my fellows, what should I say to you? / Let me be recorded by the righteous gods, / I am as poor as you.
Alas, my friends, what can I say to you? Let the righteous gods record it: I'm as poor as you are.
Such a house broke! / So noble a master fall'n! All gone! and not / One friend to take his fortune by the arm / And go along with him!
Such a great house broken! So noble a master fallen! All gone! And not one friend to take his fortune by the arm and go along with him!

As we do turn our backs / From our companion, thrown into his grave, / So his familiars to his buried fortunes / Slink all away, leave their false vows with him, / Like empty purses pick'd; and his poor self, / A dedicated beggar to the air, / With his disease of all-shunn'd poverty, / Walks, like contempt, alone. More of our fellows.

Just as we turn our backs on a companion once he's thrown into his grave, so his close friends all slink away from his buried fortune, leaving their false vows with him like empty, picked purses. And he himself, a beggar given over to the open air, with his disease of poverty that everyone avoids, walks alone, like scorn itself. More of our fellows.
All broken implements of a ruin'd house.
All broken tools of a ruined house.

Yet do our hearts wear Timon's livery, / That see I by our faces; we are fellows still, / Serving alike in sorrow. Leak'd is our bark, / And we, poor mates, stand on the dying deck, / Hearing the surges threat: we must all part / Into this sea of air.

Yet our hearts still wear Timon's uniform; I can see that in our faces. We are still fellows, serving together in sorrow. Our ship has sprung a leak, and we poor crewmen stand on the sinking deck, hearing the waves threaten. We must all part into this sea of air.

Good fellows all, / The latest of my wealth I'll share amongst you. / Wherever we shall meet, for Timon's sake / Let's yet be fellows; let's shake our heads, and say, / As 'twere a knell unto our master's fortune, / 'We have seen better days.' Let each take some;

Good fellows all, I'll share the last of my money among you. Wherever we meet, for Timon's sake, let's still be friends. Let's shake our heads and say, as if it were a funeral bell for our master's fortune, "We have seen better days." Each of you take some.
Nay, put out all your hands. Not one word more: / Thus part we rich in sorrow, parting poor.
No, hold out all your hands. Not another word. So we part rich in sorrow, though poor.

O! the fierce wretchedness that glory brings us. / Who would not wish to be from wealth exempt, / Since riches point to misery and contempt? / Who would be so mock'd with glory? or so live, / But in a dream of friendship? / To have his pomp, and all what state compounds / But only painted, like his varnish'd friends? / Poor honest lord! brought low by his own heart, / Undone by goodness. Strange, unusual blood, / When man's worst sin is he does too much good! / Who then dares to be half so kind agen? / For bounty, that makes gods, does still mar men. / My dearest lord, bless'd, to be most accurs'd, / Rich, only to be wretched, thy great fortunes / Are made thy chief afflictions. Alas! kind lord, / He's flung in rage from this ingrateful seat / Of monstrous friends; / Nor has he with him to supply his life, / Or that which can command it. / I'll follow and enquire him out: / I'll ever serve his mind with my best will; / Whilst I have gold, I'll be his steward still.

Oh, the terrible misery that greatness brings us! Who wouldn't wish to be free of wealth, since riches lead to misery and contempt? Who would want to be fooled by glory like this, or to live only in a dream of friendship, to have his splendour and everything that makes up high rank only painted on, like his varnished friends? Poor honest lord! Brought low by his own heart, ruined by goodness. What a strange, unnatural temperament, when a man's worst sin is doing too much good! Who will dare to be half so kind again? Generosity, which makes gods, still ruins men. My dearest lord, blessed only to be cursed the more, rich only to be wretched, your great fortune has become your chief affliction. Alas, kind lord! He has rushed off in a rage from this ungrateful home of monstrous friends, and he has nothing with him to keep himself alive, or money to buy it. I'll follow and find out where he is. I'll always serve his wishes with all my goodwill. As long as I have gold, I'll still be his steward.

O blessed breeding sun! draw from the earth / Rotten humidity; below thy sister's orb / Infect the air! Twinn'd brothers of one womb, / Whose procreation, residence and birth, / Scarce is dividant, touch them with several fortunes; / The greater scorns the lesser: not nature, / To whom all sores lay siege, can bear great fortune, / But by contempt of nature. / Raise me this beggar, and deny't that lord; / The senator shall bear contempt hereditary, / The beggar native honour. / It is the pasture lards the rother's sides, / The want that makes him lean. Who dares, who dares, / In purity of manhood stand upright, / And say, 'This man's a flatterer'? if one be, / So are they all; for every grize of fortune / Is smooth'd by that below: the learned pate / Ducks to the golden fool: all is oblique; / There's nothing level in our cursed natures / But direct villainy. Therefore, be abhorr'd / All feasts, societies, and throngs of men! / His semblable, yea, himself, Timon disdains: / Destruction fang mankind! Earth, yield me roots!

Oh blessed, life-giving sun, draw rotten damp up from the earth and infect the air below the moon! Take twin brothers from one womb, whose conception, life in the womb and birth can hardly be told apart, and give them different fortunes: the greater will scorn the lesser. Human nature, besieged by every ill, can't bear great fortune without despising its own kind. Raise this beggar up and take that lord's wealth away: the senator will be born to contempt, the beggar to honour. It's the pasture that fattens the ox's sides, and the lack of it that makes him thin. Who dares, who dares to stand up straight in pure manliness and say "This man is a flatterer"? If one is, they all are, because every step on fortune's stair is smoothed by the one below. The learned head bows to the golden fool. Everything is crooked. There's nothing straight in our cursed natures except outright villainy. So let all feasts, gatherings and crowds of men be hated! Timon despises his fellow man, yes, even himself. May destruction seize mankind in its teeth! Earth, give me roots!

Who seeks for better of thee, sauce his palate / With thy most operant poison! What is here? / Gold! yellow, glittering, precious gold! No, gods, / I am no idle votarist. Roots, you clear heavens! / Thus much of this will make black white, foul fair, / Wrong right, base noble, old young, coward valiant. / Ha! you gods, why this? What this, you gods? Why, this / Will lug your priests and servants from your sides, / Pluck stout men's pillows from below their head: / This yellow slave / Will knit and break religions; bless the accurs'd, / Make the hoar leprosy ador'd; place thieves, / And give them title, knee, and approbation, / With senators on the bench; this is it / That makes the wappen'd widow wed again; / She, whom the spital-house and ulcerous sores / Would cast the gorge at, this embalms and spices / To the April day again. Come, damned earth, / Thou common whore of mankind, that putt'st odds / Among the rout of nations, I will make thee / Do thy right nature.—[March afar off] / Ha! a drum? thou'rt quick, / But yet I'll bury thee: thou'lt go, strong thief, / When gouty keepers of thee cannot stand: / Nay, stay thou out for earnest.

Whoever wants something better from you, may you season his taste with your strongest poison! What's this? Gold! Yellow, glittering, precious gold! No, gods, I'm not a half-hearted worshipper: I asked for roots, you clear heavens! This much of it will make black white, foul fair, wrong right, low noble, old young, coward brave. Ha, you gods! Why this? What's this for, you gods? Why, this will drag your priests and servants away from your side and pull pillows from under the heads of strong men who are still alive. This yellow slave will tie religions together and break them apart, bless the cursed, make white leprosy adored, place thieves among senators on the bench and give them titles, bowing and approval. This is what makes the worn-out widow marry again. Her, whom a hospital full of ulcerous patients would vomit at the sight of, this perfumes and spices back to the freshness of an April day. Come, damned earth, you common whore of mankind who sets nations quarrelling, I will make you do what your nature is. (Marching heard in the distance) Ha! A drum? You're lively, but I'll bury you all the same. You'll walk about, strong thief, when your gouty keepers can't stand. No, stay out here as a down payment.
A beast, as thou art. The canker gnaw thy heart, / For showing me again the eyes of man!
A beast, as you are. May a cancer eat your heart for showing me the eyes of man again!
What is thy name? Is man so hateful to thee, / That art thyself a man?
What's your name? Is man so hateful to you, when you're a man yourself?
I am Misanthropos, and hate mankind. / For thy part, I do wish thou wert a dog, / That I might love thee something.
I am Misanthropos, the man-hater, and I hate mankind. As for you, I wish you were a dog, so that I could love you a little.
I know thee well, / But in thy fortunes am unlearn'd and strange.
I know you well, but I know nothing about what has happened to you.

I know thee too; and more than that I know thee / I not desire to know. Follow thy drum; / With man's blood paint the ground, gules, gules; / Religious canons, civil laws are cruel; / Then what should war be? This fell whore of thine / Hath in her more destruction than thy sword / For all her cherubin look.

I know you too, and I don't want to know you any better than that. Follow your drum. Paint the ground red, red, with man's blood. The church's rules and the civil laws are cruel, so what should war be? This deadly whore of yours carries more destruction in her than your sword, for all her angelic looks.
I will not kiss thee; then the rot returns / To thine own lips again.
I won't kiss you, so the rot goes back to your own lips.
How came the noble Timon to this change?
How did the noble Timon come to change like this?
As the moon does, by wanting light to give: / But then renew I could not like the moon; / There were no suns to borrow of.
As the moon does, by having no more light to give. But I couldn't renew myself like the moon: there were no suns to borrow light from.
Noble Timon, / What friendship may I do thee?
Noble Timon, what act of friendship can I do for you?
None, but to maintain my opinion.
None, except to support my opinion.
Promise me friendship, but perform none: if thou wilt not / promise, the gods plague thee, for thou art man! If thou dost / perform, confound thee, for thou art a man!
Promise me friendship, but don't carry it out. If you won't promise, may the gods plague you, because you're a man! If you do carry it out, may they destroy you, because you're a man!
I have heard in some sort of thy miseries.
I have heard something of your misfortunes.
Thou saw'st them when I had prosperity.
You saw them when I was prosperous.
I see them now; then was a blessed time.
I see them now. Then was a blessed time.
As thine is now, held with a brace of harlots.
As yours is now, held fast by a pair of harlots.
Is this the Athenian minion whom the world / Voic'd so regardfully?
Is this the Athenian favourite the world spoke of so respectfully?

Be a whore still; they love thee not that use thee; / Give them diseases, leaving with thee their lust. / Make use of thy salt hours; season the slaves / For tubs and baths; bring down rose-cheeked youth / To the tub-fast and the diet.

Stay a whore. The men who use you don't love you. Give them diseases in return for the lust they leave with you. Make the most of your lecherous hours. Prepare the slaves for the sweating tubs and baths that cure the pox. Bring rosy-cheeked young men down to the tub, the fasting and the diet.

Pardon him, sweet Timandra, for his wits / Are drown'd and lost in his calamities. / I have but little gold of late, brave Timon, / The want whereof doth daily make revolt / In my penurious band: I have heard, and griev'd / How cursed Athens, mindless of thy worth, / Forgetting thy great deeds, when neighbour states, / But for thy sword and fortune, trod upon them,—

Forgive him, sweet Timandra, because his mind is drowned and lost in his misfortunes. I've had little gold lately, brave Timon, and the lack of it causes mutiny every day in my poor army. I have heard, and grieved, how cursed Athens, forgetting your worth and your great deeds, when neighbouring states would have trampled on it but for your sword and your wealth...
I prithee, beat thy drum, and get thee gone.
Please, beat your drum and go away.
I am thy friend, and pity thee, dear Timon.
I'm your friend, and I pity you, dear Timon.
How dost thou pity him whom thou dost trouble? / I had rather be alone.
How can you pity a man you are pestering? I'd rather be alone.
Why, fare thee well: / Here is some gold for thee.
Well, goodbye. Here's some gold for you.
Keep it, I cannot eat it.
Keep it. I can't eat it.
When I have laid proud Athens on a heap,—
When I have reduced proud Athens to a heap of rubble...
Are you making war on Athens?
Yes, Timon, and I have good reason.
The gods confound them all in thy conquest; / And thee after, when thou hast conquer'd!
May the gods destroy them all through your conquest, and destroy you afterwards, when you have conquered!

That, by killing of villains, / Thou wast born to conquer my country. / Put up thy gold: go on,—here's gold,—go on; / Be as a planetary plague, when Jove / Will o'er some high-vic'd city hang his poison / In the sick air: let not thy sword skip one. / Pity not honour'd age for his white beard; / He is an usurer. Strike me the counterfeit matron; / It is her habit only that is honest, / Herself's a bawd. Let not the virgin's cheek / Make soft thy trenchant sword; for those milk paps / That through the window-bars bore at men's eyes, / Are not within the leaf of pity writ, / But set them down horrible traitors. Spare not the babe, / Whose dimpled smiles from fools exhaust their mercy; / Think it a bastard, whom the oracle / Hath doubtfully pronounc'd thy throat shall cut, / And mince it sans remorse. Swear against objects; / Put armour on thine ears and on thine eyes, / Whose proof nor yells of mothers, maids, nor babes, / Nor sight of priests in holy vestments bleeding, / Shall pierce a jot. There's gold to pay thy soldiers: / Make large confusion; and, thy fury spent, / Confounded be thyself! Speak not, be gone.

Because you were born to conquer my country by killing villains. Put away your gold. Go on; here's gold; go on. Be like a plague sent by the planets, when Jove hangs his poison in the sick air over some city deep in vice. Don't let your sword skip a single person. Don't pity old age for its white beard; he's a moneylender. Strike the respectable-looking matron; only her clothes are honest, she herself is a bawd. Don't let the virgin's cheek soften your sharp sword, because those milky breasts that peep at men through the window bars aren't written on pity's page. Count them as dreadful traitors. Don't spare the baby, whose dimpled smiles drain fools of their mercy. Think of it as a bastard whom the oracle has darkly prophesied will cut your throat, and chop it up without remorse. Swear yourself against all pitiful sights. Put armour on your ears and eyes so strong that neither the screams of mothers, girls and babies, nor the sight of priests bleeding in their holy robes, can pierce it at all. Here's gold to pay your soldiers. Cause great destruction, and when your fury is spent, may you be destroyed yourself! Don't speak. Go.
Hast thou gold yet? I'll take the gold thou giv'st me, / Not all thy counsel.
Have you still got gold? I'll take the gold you give me, but not all your advice.
Dost thou, or dost thou not, heaven's curse upon thee!
Whether you do or not, heaven's curse on you!
Give us some gold, good Timon: / Hast thou more?
Give us some gold, good Timon. Have you got more?

Enough to make a whore forswear her trade, / And to make whores a bawd. Hold up, you sluts, / Your aprons mountant: you are not oathable, / Although, I know, you'll swear, terribly swear / Into strong shudders and to heavenly agues, / The immortal gods that hear you, spare your oaths, / I'll trust to your conditions: be whores still; / And he whose pious breath seeks to convert you, / Be strong in whore, allure him, burn him up; / Let your close fire predominate his smoke, / And be no turncoats: yet may your pains, six months, / Be quite contrary: and thatch your poor thin roofs / With burdens of the dead; some that were hang'd, / No matter; wear them, betray with them: whore still; / Paint till a horse may mire upon your face: / A pox of wrinkles!

Enough to make a whore give up her trade, and to make whores into bawds. Hold up your aprons, you sluts. You can't be trusted to swear an oath, though I know you'll swear, swear terribly enough to make the immortal gods who hear you shudder and shake with fever. Spare your oaths; I'll trust your natures. Stay whores. And if some preacher's pious breath tries to convert you, be strong in whoring, seduce him and burn him up. Let your secret fire overpower his smoky sermon, and don't change sides. Yet for six months of the year may your efforts go the other way, suffering the pox yourselves. Thatch your thin, balding heads with wigs taken from the dead, some of them hanged men, no matter; wear them and deceive with them. Stay whores. Paint your faces so thick that a horse could get stuck in the mud on them. A pox on wrinkles!
Well, more gold. What then? / Believe't that we'll do anything for gold.
Well, more gold. What then? Believe us, we'll do anything for gold.

Consumptions sow / In hollow bones of man; strike their sharp shins, / And mar men's spurring. Crack the lawyer's voice, / That he may never more false title plead, / Nor sound his quillets shrilly; hoar the flamen, / That scolds against the quality of flesh, / And not believes himself: down with the nose, / Down with it flat; take the bridge quite away / Of him that, his particular to foresee, / Smells from the general weal: make curl'd-pate ruffians bald, / And let the unscarr'd braggarts of the war / Derive some pain from you: plague all, / That your activity may defeat and quell / The source of all erection. There's more gold; / Do you damn others, and let this damn you, / And ditches grave you all!

Sow wasting diseases in men's hollow bones. Strike their sharp shins and stop them riding. Crack the lawyer's voice so that he can never again plead a false claim or squeal out his quibbles. Make the priest hoarse, who preaches against the flesh and doesn't believe himself. Bring down the nose, flatten it, take the bridge right off the nose of the man who sniffs out his own private gain and ignores the common good. Make curly-haired thugs bald, and let the boastful soldiers who come home unscarred from war get some pain from you. Infect everyone, so that your work may destroy and kill the source of all erection. Here's more gold. You damn others, and let this damn you, and may ditches be your graves!
More counsel with more money, bounteous Timon.
More advice, with more money, generous Timon.
More whore, more mischief first; I have given you earnest.
More whoring and more mischief first. I've given you a down payment.
Strike up the drum towards Athens! Farewell, Timon: / If I thrive well, I'll visit thee again.
Beat the drum and march towards Athens! Goodbye, Timon. If I do well, I'll visit you again.
If I hope well, I'll never see thee more.
If my hopes come true, I'll never see you again.
I never did you any harm.
Yes, thou spok'st well of me.
Yes, you did. You spoke well of me.
Men daily find it. Get thee away, and take / Thy beagles with thee.
Men find it so every day. Get out, and take your hounds with you.
We're only offending him. Strike up the drum!
That nature, being sick of man's unkindness, / Should yet be hungry! Common mother, thou,
To think that nature, sick of man's unkindness, should still be hungry! You, common mother of us all,

Whose womb unmeasurable, and infinite breast, / Teems, and feeds all; whose self-same mettle, / Whereof thy proud child, arrogant man, is puff'd, / Engenders the black toad and adder blue, / The gilded newt and eyeless venom'd worm, / With all the abhorred births below crisp heaven / Whereon Hyperion's quickening fire doth shine; / Yield him, who all thy human sons doth hate, / From forth thy plenteous bosom, one poor root! / Ensear thy fertile and conceptious womb, / Let it no more bring out ingrateful man! / Go great with tigers, dragons, wolves, and bears; / Teem with new monsters, whom thy upward face / Hath to the marbled mansion all above / Never presented! O! a root; dear thanks: / Dry up thy marrows, vines and plough-torn leas; / Whereof ingrateful man, with liquorish draughts / And morsels unctuous, greases his pure mind, / That from it all consideration slips!

whose immeasurable womb and endless breast give birth to everything and feed everything, whose same material, from which your proud child, arrogant man, is puffed up, also breeds the black toad and the blue adder, the golden newt and the blind poisonous snake, with all the hateful creatures under the bright sky that the sun's life-giving fire shines on, give the man who hates all your human sons one poor root from your plentiful breast! Dry up your fertile, conceiving womb. Let it never again produce ungrateful man! Be pregnant with tigers, dragons, wolves and bears. Breed new monsters that your upturned face has never shown to the marble palace of heaven above! Oh, a root! Thank you dearly. Dry up your rich juices, your vines and ploughed fields, from which ungrateful man, with his sweet drinks and greasy food, smears over his clear mind so that all good sense slips out of it!
I was directed hither: men report / Thou dost affect my manners, and dost use them.
I was told to come here. People say you are copying my manners and imitating me.
'Tis, then, because thou dost not keep a dog / Whom I would imitate: consumption catch thee!
That's because you don't keep a dog that I could imitate instead. May you catch a wasting disease!

This is in thee a nature but infected; / A poor unmanly melancholy sprung / From change of fortune. Why this spade, this place? / This slave-like habit? and these looks of care? / Thy flatterers yet wear silk, drink wine, lie soft, / Hug their diseas'd perfumes, and have forgot / That ever Timon was. Shame not these woods / By putting on the cunning of a carper. / Be thou a flatterer now, and seek to thrive / By that which has undone thee: hinge thy knee / And let his very breath, whom thou'lt observe / Blow off thy cap; praise his most vicious strain, / And call it excellent. Thou wast told thus; / Thou gav'st thine ears, like tapsters that bade welcome, / To knaves and all approachers: 'tis most just / That thou turn rascal; hadst thou wealth again, / Rascals should have't. Do not assume my likeness.

In you this is only an infected nature, a feeble, unmanly gloom that comes from your change of fortune. Why this spade, this place, these slave's clothes, these worried looks? Your flatterers still wear silk, drink wine, sleep soft, hug their diseased perfumed women, and have forgotten that Timon ever existed. Don't shame these woods by putting on the airs of a fault-finder. Be a flatterer yourself now, and try to prosper by the very thing that has ruined you. Bend your knee as if it had a hinge, and let the mere breath of the man you court blow your cap off. Praise his worst vice and call it excellent. That's how they spoke to you. You lent your ears, like innkeepers welcoming everyone, to rogues and anyone who came along. It's only right that you should turn rascal. If you had wealth again, rascals would get it. Don't try to look like me.
Were I like thee I'd throw away myself.
If I were like you, I'd throw myself away.

Thou hast cast away thyself, being like thyself; / A madman so long, now a fool. What! think'st / That the bleak air, thy boisterous chamberlain, / Will put thy shirt on warm? will these moss'd trees, / That have outliv'd the eagle, page thy heels / And skip when thou point'st out? will the cold brook, / Candied with ice, caudle thy morning taste / To cure thy o'ernight's surfeit? Call the creatures / Whose naked natures live in all the spite / Of wreakful heaven, whose bare unhoused trunks, / To the conflicting elements expos'd, / Answer mere nature; bid them flatter thee; / O! thou shalt find—

You threw yourself away by being like yourself: a madman for so long, now a fool. What, do you think the bitter wind, your rough servant, will warm your shirt for you? Will these mossy trees, older than the eagle, follow at your heels like pages and jump when you point? Will the cold stream, iced over like sugar, make you a warm drink in the morning to cure last night's excess? Call the creatures whose naked bodies live through all the spite of avenging heaven, whose bare, homeless bodies are exposed to the warring elements and live by nature alone. Tell them to flatter you. Oh, you'll find...
I love thee better now than e'er I did.
I love you more now than I ever did.
I flatter not, but say thou art a caitiff.
I don't flatter. I say you are a wretch.
Why dost thou seek me out?
Why do you come looking for me?
Always a villain's office or a fool's. / Dost please thyself in't?
That's always the job of a villain or a fool. Do you enjoy it?

If thou didst put this sour-cold habit on / To castigate thy pride, 'twere well; but thou / Dost it enforcedly; thou'dst courtier be again / Wert thou not beggar. Willing misery / Outlives incertain pomp, is crown'd before; / The one is filling still, never complete; / The other, at high wish: best state, contentless, / Hath a distracted and most wretched being, / Worse than the worst, content. / Thou shouldst desire to die, being miserable.

If you had put on this harsh, cold way of life to punish your pride, it would be good. But you do it because you're forced to. You'd be a courtier again if you weren't a beggar. Poverty that is chosen outlives uncertain splendour and wins its crown sooner. One is always filling up and never full; the other has all it wishes. The best position, without contentment, is a troubled and wretched existence, worse than the worst position with contentment. Since you're miserable, you ought to want to die.

Not by his breath that is more miserable. / Thou art a slave, whom Fortune's tender arm / With favour never clasp'd, but bred a dog. / Hadst thou, like us from our first swath, proceeded / The sweet degrees that this brief world affords / To such as may the passive drugs of it / Freely command, thou wouldst have plung'd thyself / In general riot; melted down thy youth / In different beds of lust; and never learn'd / The icy precepts of respect, but follow'd / The sugar'd game before thee. But myself, / Who had the world as my confectionary, / The mouths, the tongues, the eyes, and hearts of men / At duty, more than I could frame employment, / That numberless upon me stuck as leaves / Do on the oak, have with one winter's brush / Fell from their boughs, and left me open, bare / For every storm that blows; I, to bear this, / That never knew but better, is some burden: / Thy nature did commence in sufferance, time / Hath made thee hard in't. Why shouldst thou hate men? / They never flatter'd thee: what hast thou given? / If thou wilt curse, thy father, that poor rag, / Must be thy subject; who in spite put stuff / To some she-beggar and compounded thee / Poor rogue hereditary. Hence! be gone! / If thou hadst not been born the worst of men, / Thou hadst been a knave and flatterer.

Not on the advice of someone more miserable than me. You're a slave whom Fortune never held lovingly in her arms, but bred as a dog. If you had gone, as I did from my baby clothes, through all the sweet stages this short life offers to those who can freely command its willing pleasures, you'd have thrown yourself into general excess, melted your youth away in different beds of lust, and never learned the icy rules of caution, but chased the sugary prey in front of you. But I, who had the world as my sweet shop, with the mouths, tongues, eyes and hearts of men at my service, more than I could find work for, who had them sticking to me in countless numbers as leaves do to the oak, have seen them fall from the branches at one brush of winter, leaving me open and bare to every storm that blows. For me, who never knew anything but better, it's a heavy burden to bear. Your life began in suffering, and time has hardened you to it. Why should you hate men? They never flattered you. What have you ever given? If you want to curse, it must be your father, that poor rag, who out of spite lay with some beggar woman and made you a born poor rogue. Get out! Go! If you hadn't been born the lowest of men, you'd have been a rogue and a flatterer.
Ay, that I am not thee.
Yes, proud that I'm not you.
I, that I was / No prodigal.
And I'm proud that I was never a spendthrift.
I, that I am one now; / Were all the wealth I have shut up in thee, / I'd give thee leave to hang it. Get thee gone. / That the whole life of Athens were in this! / Thus would I eat it.

And I'm proud that I am one now. If all the wealth I have were locked up in you, I'd give you permission to hang yourself. Go away. I wish the whole life of Athens were in this root! I'd eat it like this.
Here; I will mend thy feast.
First mend my company, take away thyself.
First improve my company: take yourself away.
So I shall mend mine own, by the lack of thine.
Then I'll improve my own company by losing yours.
'Tis not well mended so, it is but botch'd. / If not, I would it were.
That isn't improving it, it's just patching it badly. If it isn't, I wish it were.
What wouldst thou have to Athens?
What message do you want sent to Athens?
Thee thither in a whirlwind. If thou wilt, / Tell them there I have gold; look, so I have.
You, sent there in a whirlwind. If you like, tell them I have gold. Look, I do.
Here is no use for gold.
There's no use for gold here.
The best and truest; / For here it sleeps and does no hired harm.
It's the best and truest use, because here it sleeps and does no harm for hire.
Where do you sleep at night, Timon?
Under that's above me. / Where feed'st thou o' days, Apemantus?
Under what's above me. Where do you eat by day, Apemantus?
Where my stomach finds meat; or rather, where I eat it.
Wherever my stomach finds food, or rather, wherever I eat it.
Would poison were obedient and knew my mind!
I wish poison were obedient and knew what I wanted!

The middle of humanity thou never knewest, but the / extremity of both ends. When thou wast in thy gilt and thy / perfume, they mock'd thee for too much curiosity; in thy rags / thou know'st none, but art despised for the contrary. There's a / medlar for thee; eat it.

You never knew the middle way of life, only the extremes at both ends. When you were all gilt and perfume, people mocked you for being too fussy. In your rags you have no fussiness at all, and you're despised for the opposite. Here's a medlar for you; eat it.
On what I hate I feed not.
I don't eat what I hate.
Ay, though it look like thee.
Yes, even though it looks like you.
An thou hadst hated medlars sooner, thou shouldst have loved / thyself better now. What man didst thou ever know unthrift / that was beloved after his means?
If you had hated meddlers sooner, you'd love yourself more now. What spendthrift did you ever know who was loved once his money was gone?
Who, without those means thou talkest of, didst thou ever / know beloved?
And who did you ever know who was loved without the money you're talking about?
I understand thee; thou hadst some means to keep a dog.
I understand you: you had enough money to keep a dog that loved you.
What things in the world canst thou nearest compare to / thy flatterers?
What things in the world can you compare most closely to your flatterers?
Women nearest; but men, men are the things themselves. What / wouldst thou do with the world, Apemantus, if it lay in thy / power?
Women, most closely. But men, men are the very things themselves. What would you do with the world, Apemantus, if you had power over it?
Give it the beasts, to be rid of the men.
Give it to the beasts, to be rid of the men.
Wouldst thou have thyself fall in the confusion of men, and / remain a beast with the beasts?
Would you let yourself fall with the ruin of men, and stay on as a beast among the beasts?

A beastly ambition, which the gods grant thee to attain to. / If thou wert the lion, the fox would beguile thee; if thou wert / the lamb, the fox would eat thee; if thou wert the fox, the lion / would suspect thee, when peradventure, thou wert accused by the / ass; if thou wert the ass, thy dulness would torment thee, and / still thou livedst but as a breakfast to the wolf; if thou wert / the wolf, thy greediness would afflict thee, and oft thou / shouldst hazard thy life for thy dinner; wert thou the unicorn, / pride and wrath would confound thee and make thine own self the / conquest of thy fury; wert thou a bear, thou wouldst be killed by / the horse; wert thou a horse, thou wouldst be seized by the / leopard; wert thou a leopard, thou wert german to the lion, and / the spots of thy kindred were jurors on thy life; all thy safety / were remotion, and thy defence absence. What beast couldst thou / be that were not subject to a beast? and what beast art thou / already, that seest not thy loss in transformation!

A beastly ambition, and may the gods let you achieve it. If you were the lion, the fox would trick you. If you were the lamb, the fox would eat you. If you were the fox, the lion would suspect you whenever, perhaps, the ass accused you. If you were the ass, your stupidity would torment you, and you'd still live only as the wolf's breakfast. If you were the wolf, your greed would plague you, and you'd often risk your life for your dinner. If you were the unicorn, pride and rage would ruin you and make you the victim of your own fury. If you were a bear, the horse would kill you. If you were a horse, the leopard would seize you. If you were a leopard, you'd be a cousin of the lion, and your relatives' spots would be the jury that condemned you. Your only safety would be distance, and your only defence absence. What beast could you be that wasn't prey to another beast? And what a beast you are already, not to see how much you'd lose by the change!
If thou couldst please me with speaking to me, thou / mightst have hit upon it here; the commonwealth of Athens is / become a forest of beasts.
If you could ever please me by talking to me, you might have done it now. The state of Athens has become a forest of beasts.
How has the ass broke the wall, that thou art out of the / city?
How did the ass break down the city wall, so that you're outside the city?
Yonder comes a poet and a painter: the plague of company / light upon thee! I will fear to catch it, and give way. When I / know not what else to do, I'll see thee again.
Over there comes a poet and a painter. May the plague of company land on you! I'm afraid of catching it, so I'll get out of the way. When I don't know what else to do, I'll come and see you again.
When there is nothing living but thee, thou shalt be / welcome. I had rather be a beggar's dog than Apemantus.
When there's nothing alive but you, you'll be welcome. I'd rather be a beggar's dog than Apemantus.
Thou art the cap of all the fools alive.
You're the king of all the fools alive.
Would thou wert clean enough to spit upon!
I wish you were clean enough to spit on!
A plague on thee! thou art too bad to curse!
A plague on you! You're too bad to curse!
All villains that do stand by thee are pure.
All villains are pure compared with you.
There is no leprosy but what thou speak'st.
There's no leprosy except what you speak.
If I name thee, / I'll beat thee, but I should infect my hands.
If I named you, that would be a curse. I'd beat you, but I'd infect my hands.
I would my tongue could rot them off!
I wish my tongue could rot them off!
Away, thou issue of a mangy dog! / Choler does kill me that thou art alive; / I swound to see thee.
Get away, you son of a mangy dog! It's killing me with anger that you're alive. I faint to see you.
Away, / Thou tedious rogue! I am sorry I shall lose / A stone by thee.
Away, you tedious rogue! I'm sorry I'll waste a stone on you.

Rogue, rogue, rogue! / I am sick of this false world, and will love nought / But even the mere necessities upon't. / Then, Timon, presently prepare thy grave; / Lie where the light foam of the sea may beat / Thy gravestone daily: make thine epitaph, / That death in me at others' lives may laugh.

Rogue, rogue, rogue! I'm sick of this false world, and will love nothing in it but the bare necessities. Then, Timon, get your grave ready at once. Lie where the light sea foam can beat on your gravestone every day. Write your epitaph, so that in my death I can laugh at other people's lives.

O thou sweet king-killer, and dear divorce / 'Twixt natural son and sire! thou bright defiler / Of Hymen's purest bed! thou valiant Mars! / Thou ever young, fresh, lov'd, and delicate wooer, / Whose blush doth thaw the consecrated snow / That lies on Dian's lap! thou visible god, / That solder'st close impossibilities, / And mak'st them kiss! that speak'st with every tongue / To every purpose! O thou touch of hearts! / Think, thy slave man rebels, and by thy virtue / Set them into confounding odds, that beasts / May have the world in empire!

Oh you sweet killer of kings, and dear divider of a natural son from his father! You bright defiler of the purest marriage bed! You brave Mars! You ever young, fresh, loved and delicate suitor, whose blush melts the holy snow that lies in Diana's lap! You visible god, who welds together things that could never meet and makes them kiss! You who speak every language for every purpose! Oh you touchstone of hearts! Imagine that man, your slave, is rebelling, and by your power set men fighting among themselves until they destroy each other, so that the beasts may rule the world!
Would 'twere so: / But not till I am dead; I'll say thou'st gold: / Thou wilt be throng'd to shortly.
I wish it were so, but not until I'm dead. I'll tell people you have gold. You'll soon be mobbed.
Long live so, and so die!
Live long like that, and die like that!
I am quit. / More things like men! Eat, Timon, and abhor them.
I'm rid of him. More things that look like men! Eat, Timon, and loathe them.
Where should he have this gold? It is some poor / fragment, some slender ort of his remainder. The mere want of / gold, and the falling-from of his friends, drove him into this / melancholy.
Where would he get this gold? It must be some poor scrap, some thin leftover of what he had. It was just the lack of gold and his friends' desertion that drove him into this gloom.
It is noised he hath a mass of treasure.
Word is he has a heap of treasure.
Let us make the assay upon him: if he care not for't, / he will supply us easily; if he covetously reserve it, how / shall's get it?
Let's try him. If he doesn't care about it, he'll give it to us easily. If he greedily hoards it, how shall we get it?
True; for he bears it not about him, 'tis hid.
True, because he doesn't carry it on him. It's hidden.
Both of those, and sons of women too.
We are not thieves, but men that much do want.
We're not thieves, but men in great need.

Your greatest want is, you want much of meat. / Why should you want? Behold, the earth hath roots; / Within this mile break forth a hundred springs; / The oaks bear mast, the briars scarlet hips; / The bounteous housewife, Nature, on each bush / Lays her full mess before you. Want! Why want?

Your greatest need is that you need a lot of food. Why should you be in need? Look, the earth has roots. Within a mile of here a hundred springs burst out. The oaks bear acorns, the briars red rosehips. Nature, the generous housewife, sets out a full meal for you on every bush. Need! Why are you in need?
We cannot live on grass, on berries, water, / As beasts and birds and fishes.
We can't live on grass, berries and water, like beasts and birds and fish.

Nor on the beasts themselves, the birds, and fishes; / You must eat men. Yet thanks I must you con / That you are thieves profess'd, that you work not / In holier shapes; for there is boundless theft / In limited professions. Rascal thieves, / Here's gold. Go, suck the subtle blood o' the grape / Till the high fever seethe your blood to froth, / And so scape hanging: trust not the physician; / His antidotes are poison, and he slays / More than you rob: take wealth and lives together; / Do villainy, do, since you protest to do't, / Like workmen. I'll example you with thievery: / The sun's a thief, and with his great attraction / Robs the vast sea; the moon's an arrant thief, / And her pale fire she snatches from the sun; / The sea's a thief, whose liquid surge resolves / The moon into salt tears; the earth's a thief, / That feeds and breeds by a composture stolen / From general excrement, each thing's a thief; / The laws, your curb and whip, in their rough power / Has uncheck'd theft. Love not yourselves; away! / Rob one another. There's more gold; cut throats; / All that you meet are thieves. To Athens go, / Break open shops; nothing can you steal / But thieves do lose it: steal no less for this / I give you; and gold confound you howsoe'er! / Amen.

Nor on the beasts themselves, the birds and fish. You have to eat men. Still, I must thank you for being open, professional thieves and not working in holier disguises, because there is boundless theft in the respectable professions. Rascal thieves, here's gold. Go, suck the subtle blood of the grape until the high fever boils your blood to froth, and so escape hanging. Don't trust the doctor: his medicines are poison, and he kills more men than you rob. Take wealth and lives together. Do villainy, since you profess to do it, like true craftsmen. I'll give you examples of thieving. The sun is a thief, and with his great pull he robs the vast sea. The moon is an outright thief, and snatches her pale fire from the sun. The sea is a thief, whose liquid waves dissolve the moon into salt tears. The earth is a thief, which feeds and breeds on manure stolen from everything's excrement. Everything is a thief. The laws, your bridle and your whip, commit unchecked theft with their rough power. Don't love yourselves. Go! Rob one another. Here's more gold. Cut throats. Everyone you meet is a thief. Go to Athens, break open shops. You can steal nothing that a thief doesn't lose. Don't steal any less because of what I give you, and may gold destroy you anyway! Amen.
Has almost charm'd me from my profession by / persuading me to it.
He has almost charmed me out of my profession by urging me to follow it.
'Tis in the malice of mankind that he thus advises / us; not to have us thrive in our mystery.
It's out of hatred for mankind that he advises us like this, not so that we'll succeed in our trade.
I'll believe him as an enemy, and give over my trade.
I'll believe him as I would an enemy, and give up my trade.
Let us first see peace in Athens. There is no time so / miserable but a man may be true.
Let's wait until there's peace in Athens first. No time is so wretched that a man can't be honest.

O you gods! / Is yond despised and ruinous man my lord? / Full of decay and failing? O monument / And wonder of good deeds evilly bestow'd! / What an alteration of honour / Has desperate want made! / What viler thing upon the earth than friends / Who can bring noblest minds to basest ends! / How rarely does it meet with this time's guise, / When man was wish'd to love his enemies! / Grant I may ever love, and rather woo / Those that would mischief me than those that do! / He has caught me in his eye: I will present / My honest grief unto him; and, as my lord, / Still serve him with my life. My dearest master!

Oh you gods! Is that despised, ruined man over there my lord? So wasted and failing? Oh, monument and wonder of good deeds badly placed! What a change in an honourable man desperate poverty has made! What on earth is viler than friends who can bring the noblest minds to the lowest ends! How well this suits the fashion of our times, when man was told to love his enemies! Grant that I may always love, and rather court those who openly mean me harm than those who do me harm while pretending friendship! He has seen me. I'll show him my honest grief and still serve him as my lord with my life. My dearest master!
Why dost ask that? I have forgot all men; / Then, if thou grant'st thou'rt a man, I have forgot thee.
Why do you ask that? I have forgotten all men. So, if you admit you're a man, I have forgotten you.
An honest poor servant of yours.
An honest, poor servant of yours.
Then I know thee not: / I never had honest man about me; ay all / I kept were knaves, to serve in meat to villains.
Then I don't know you. I never had an honest man around me. All the men I kept were rogues who served food to villains.
The gods are witness, / Ne'er did poor steward wear a truer grief / For his undone lord than mine eyes for you.
The gods are my witness, no poor steward ever grieved more truly for his ruined lord than my eyes grieve for you.

What! dost thou weep? Come nearer. Then I love thee, / Because thou art a woman, and disclaim'st / Flinty mankind, whose eyes do never give / But thorough lust and laughter. Pity's sleeping: / Strange times, that weep with laughing, not with weeping!

What, are you crying? Come closer. Then I love you, because you are a woman and disown hard-hearted mankind, whose eyes never water except from lust or laughter. Pity is asleep. Strange times, that weep from laughing, not from weeping!
I beg of you to know me, good my lord, / To accept my grief, and whilst this poor wealth lasts / To entertain me as your steward still.
I beg you to recognise me, my good lord, to accept my grief, and, while this little money lasts, to keep me on as your steward still.

Had I a steward / So true, so just, and now so comfortable? / It almost turns my dangerous nature mild. / Let me behold thy face. Surely, this man / Was born of woman. / Forgive my general and exceptless rashness, / You perpetual sober gods! I do proclaim / One honest man, mistake me not, but one; / No more, I pray, and he's a steward. / How fain would I have hated all mankind! / And thou redeem'st thyself: but all, save thee, / I fell with curses. / Methinks thou art more honest now than wise; / For, by oppressing and betraying me, / Thou mightst have sooner got another service: / For many so arrive at second masters / Upon their first lord's neck. But tell me true,— / For I must ever doubt, though ne'er so sure,— / Is not thy kindness subtle, covetous, / If not a usuring kindness and as rich men deal gifts, / Expecting in return, twenty for one?

Did I have a steward so loyal, so honest, and now such a comfort? It almost turns my savage nature mild. Let me look at your face. Surely this man was born of woman. Forgive my sweeping, exceptionless rashness, you eternally calm gods! I declare one honest man (don't mistake me, only one, no more, I beg you) and he is a steward. How gladly I would have hated all mankind! And you save yourself from it. But everyone except you I strike down with curses. I think you're more honest than wise now, because by oppressing and betraying me you could have found another job sooner. Many men climb to a second master over their first lord's neck. But tell me truly, for I must always doubt, however sure I am: isn't your kindness cunning and greedy, a moneylender's kindness, like rich men giving gifts and expecting twenty in return for one?

No, my most worthy master, in whose breast / Doubt and suspect, alas! are plac'd too late! / You should have fear'd false times when you did feast; / Suspect still comes where an estate is least. / That which I show, heaven knows, is merely love, / Duty and zeal to your unmatched mind, / Care of your food and living; and, believe it, / My most honour'd lord, / For any benefit that points to me, / Either in hope or present, I'd exchange / For this one wish, that you had power and wealth / To requite me by making rich yourself.

No, my most worthy master, in whose heart doubt and suspicion have, alas, been placed too late! You should have feared false times while you were feasting. Suspicion always comes when wealth is at its lowest. What I show, heaven knows, is pure love, duty and devotion to your unmatched mind, and care for your food and livelihood. And believe me, my most honoured lord, I would exchange any benefit to me, now or in the future, for this one wish: that you had the power and wealth to repay me by making yourself rich.

Look thee, 'tis so! Thou singly honest man, / Here, take: the gods, out of my misery, / Have sent thee treasure. Go, live rich and happy, / But thus condition'd: thou shalt build from men; / Hate all, curse all, show charity to none, / But let the famish'd flesh slide from the bone, / Ere thou relieve the beggar; give to dogs / What thou deny'st to men; let prisons swallow 'em, / Debts wither 'em to nothing; be men like blasted woods, / And may diseases lick up their false bloods! / And so, farewell and thrive.

Look, it is so! You single honest man, here, take this. The gods have sent you treasure out of my misery. Go, live rich and happy, but on this condition: you shall build your house far from men.
