Hate everyone, curse everyone, show charity to no one, but let starving flesh slide off the bone before you help a beggar. Give to dogs what you refuse to men. Let prisons swallow them and debts wither them to nothing. Let men be like blighted woods, and may diseases lick up their false blood! And so, goodbye, and prosper.
O! let me stay / And comfort you, my master.
Oh, let me stay and comfort you, my master.
If thou hatest curses, / Stay not; fly, whilst thou'rt bless'd and free: / Ne'er see thou man, and let me ne'er see thee.
If you hate curses, don't stay. Run, while you're blessed and free. Never see man again, and let me never see you.
As I took note of the place, it cannot be far where he / abides.
From what I noticed of the place, he can't be living far away.
What's to be thought of him? Does the rumour hold for true that / he is so full of gold?
What should we think of him? Is the rumour true that he has so much gold?
Certain. Alcibiades reports it; Phrynia and Timandra had / gold of him: he likewise enriched poor straggling soldiers with / great quantity. 'Tis said he gave unto his steward a mighty sum.
Certainly. Alcibiades says so. Phrynia and Timandra got gold from him. He also made poor stray soldiers rich with a great quantity. They say he gave his steward a huge sum.
Then this breaking of his has been but a try for his friends?
Then this bankruptcy of his was only a test of his friends?

Nothing else. You shall see him a palm in Athens again, / and flourish with the highest. Therefore 'tis not amiss we tender / our loves to him in this supposed distress of his; it will show / honestly in us, and is very likely to load our purposes with what / they travail for, if it be just and true report that goes of his / having.

Nothing else. You'll see him flourish like a palm tree in Athens again, among the highest. So it won't be a bad idea to offer him our love in this supposed hardship of his. It will look honest in us, and it's very likely to load our ambitions with what they're working for, if the reports of his wealth are true.
What have you now to present unto him?
What have you got to give him now?
Nothing at this time but my visitation; only, I will / promise him an excellent piece.
Nothing at the moment except my visit. I'll just promise him an excellent painting.
I must serve him so too, tell him of an intent that's coming / toward him.
I must do the same with him: tell him about a work I'm planning for him.

Good as the best. Promising is the very air o' the time; / it opens the eyes of expectation. Performance is ever the duller / for his act, and, but in the plainer and simpler kind of people, / the deed of saying is quite out of use. To promise is most / courtly and fashionable; performance is a kind of will or / testament which argues a great sickness in his judgment that / makes it.

The best plan. Promising is the very fashion of the times; it opens the eyes of expectation. Doing is always duller once it's done, and, except among plainer and simpler people, keeping your word is quite out of fashion. Promising is most courtly and fashionable. Doing is like making a will: it shows the man who does it has a great sickness in his judgement.
[Aside] Excellent workman! Thou canst not paint a man so bad / as is thyself.
(Aside) Excellent workman! You can't paint a man as bad as you are yourself.

I am thinking what I shall say I have provided for him. It / must be a personating of himself; a satire against the softness / of prosperity, with a discovery of the infinite flatteries that / follow youth and opulency.
I'm thinking what I'll say I've prepared for him. It must be a portrait of himself: a satire against the softness of prosperity, exposing the endless flatteries that follow youth and wealth.
[Aside] Must thou needs stand for a villain in thine own / work? Wilt thou whip thine own faults in other men? Do so, I have / gold for thee.
(Aside) Must you play the villain in your own work? Will you whip your own faults in other men? Do so; I have gold for you.
Nay, let's seek him; / Then do we sin against our own estate / When we may profit meet, and come too late.
Come, let's look for him. We sin against our own interests if we come too late when we could meet with profit.
True; / When the day serves, before black-corner'd night, / Find what thou want'st by free and offer'd light. / Come.
True. While the day lasts, before black, secret night, find what you want by the free light on offer. Come.

[Aside] I'll meet you at the turn. What a god's gold, / That he is worshipp'd in a baser temple / Than where swine feed! / 'Tis thou that rigg'st the bark and plough'st the foam, / Settlest admired reverence in a slave. / To thee be worship! and thy saints for aye / Be crown'd with plagues, that thee alone obey! / Fit I meet them.

(Aside) I'll meet you at the corner. What a god gold is, that he's worshipped in a temple lower than a pigsty! It's you that rigs the ship and ploughs the sea foam, and makes men admire and revere a slave. Worship to you! And may your saints, who obey you alone, be crowned with plagues forever! It's time I met them.
Have I once liv'd to see two honest men?
Have I lived to see two honest men?

Sir, / Having often of your open bounty tasted, / Hearing you were retir'd, your friends fall'n off, / Whose thankless natures—O abhorred spirits! / Not all the whips of heaven are large enough— / What! to you, / Whose star-like nobleness gave life and influence / To their whole being! I am rapt, and cannot cover / The monstrous bulk of this ingratitude / With any size of words.

Sir, having often enjoyed your open generosity, and hearing that you had withdrawn and that your friends had deserted you, whose ungrateful natures (oh, hateful spirits! not all the whips of heaven are big enough) what, to you, whose starlike nobility gave life and power to their whole being! I'm overcome and cannot cover the monstrous size of this ingratitude with words of any size.
Let it go naked: men may see't the better. / You, that are honest, by being what you are, / Make them best seen and known.
Let it go naked; men can see it better that way. You who are honest, by being what you are, show them up best.
He and myself / Have travail'd in the great shower of your gifts, / And sweetly felt it.
He and I have walked in the great shower of your gifts and felt it sweetly.
We are hither come to offer you our service.
We have come here to offer you our service.
Most honest men! Why, how shall I requite you? / Can you eat roots, and drink cold water? No?
Most honest men! Now, how shall I repay you? Can you eat roots and drink cold water? No?
What we can do, we'll do, to do you service.
Whatever we can do, we'll do, to serve you.
Ye're honest men! Ye've heard that I have gold; / I am sure you have. Speak truth; ye're honest men.
You're honest men! You've heard that I have gold. I'm sure you have. Tell the truth; you're honest men.
So it is said, my noble lord; but therefore / Came not my friend nor I.
So people say, my noble lord, but that isn't why my friend and I came.
Good honest men! Thou draw'st a counterfeit / Best in all Athens. Thou'rt, indeed, the best; / Thou counterfeit'st most lively.
Good honest men! You paint the best likeness in all Athens. You really are the best. You fake most lifelike.
E'en so, sir, as I say.

And for thy fiction, / Why, thy verse swells with stuff so fine and smooth / That thou art even natural in thine art. / But for all this, my honest-natur'd friends, / I must needs say you have a little fault. / Marry, 'tis not monstrous in you; neither wish I / You take much pains to mend.

And as for your fiction, why, your verse swells with matter so fine and smooth that your art is second nature to you. But for all this, my honest friends, I must say you have one small fault. It isn't monstrous in you, of course, and I don't want you to take much trouble to correct it.
Beseech your honour / To make it known to us.
We beg your honour to tell us what it is.
There's never a one of you but trusts a knave / That mightily deceives you.
Each one of you trusts a rogue who deceives you terribly.
Ay, and you hear him cog, see him dissemble, / Know his gross patchery, love him, feed him, / Keep in your bosom; yet remain assur'd / That he's a made-up villain.
Yes, and you hear him cheat, see him pretend, know all his crude deceit, and yet you love him, feed him, keep him close to your heart, while being quite sure he's a complete villain.
I know not such, my lord.
I don't know anyone like that, my lord.

Look you, I love you well; I'll give you gold, / Rid me these villains from your companies. / Hang them or stab them, drown them in a draught, / Confound them by some course, and come to me, / I'll give you gold enough.

Look, I love you well. I'll give you gold if you rid your company of these villains. Hang them or stab them, drown them in a sewer, destroy them some way, and come to me. I'll give you plenty of gold.
Name them, my lord; let's know them.
Name them, my lord. Tell us who they are.
You that way, and you this, but two in company; / Each man apart, all single and alone, / Yet an arch-villain keeps him company.
You go that way, and you this way: still two of you together. Each of you on his own, single and alone, still has an arch-villain for company.
If, where thou art, two villains shall not be, / Come not near him.
(To the Painter) If you don't want two villains where you are, don't go near him.
If thou wouldst not reside / But where one villain is, then him abandon. / Hence! pack! there's gold; you came for gold, ye slaves.
(To the Poet) If you won't live anywhere except where there's only one villain, then leave him. Get out! Clear off! There's gold. You came for gold, you slaves.
You have work for me; there's payment; hence!
(To the Painter) You did work for me; there's your payment. Go!
You are an alchemist; make gold of that. / Out, rascal dogs!
(To the Poet) You're an alchemist; make gold out of that. Out, you rascal dogs!
It is vain that you would speak with Timon; / For he is set so only to himself / That nothing but himself, which looks like man, / Is friendly with him.
It's no use trying to speak with Timon. He's so wrapped up in himself that nothing that looks like a man is friendly with him except himself.
Bring us to his cave. / It is our part and promise to the Athenians / To speak with Timon.
Take us to his cave. We have promised the Athenians, and it's our duty, to speak with Timon.

At all times alike / Men are not still the same; 'twas time and griefs / That fram'd him thus. Time, with his fairer hand, / Offering the fortunes of his former days, / The former man may make him. Bring us to him, / And chance it as it may.

Men aren't always the same at all times. It was time and griefs that made him like this. Time, with a kinder hand, offering him the fortunes of his earlier days, may make him the man he was. Take us to him, and let what happens happen.
Here is his cave. / Peace and content be here! Lord Timon! Timon! / Look out, and speak to friends. The Athenians / By two of their most reverend Senate greet thee. / Speak to them, noble Timon.
Here's his cave. Peace and contentment be here! Lord Timon! Timon! Come out and speak to friends. The Athenians greet you through two of their most respected senators. Speak to them, noble Timon.
Thou sun that comfort'st, burn! Speak and be hang'd! / For each true word, a blister! and each false / Be as a cauterizing to the root o' the tongue, / Consuming it with speaking!
You comforting sun, burn them! Speak and be hanged! For every true word you say, may you get a blister, and may every false word burn your tongue to the root, consuming it as you speak!
Of none but such as you, and you of Timon.
Worthy of nobody but people like you, and you worthy of Timon.
The senators of Athens greet thee, Timon.
The senators of Athens greet you, Timon.
I thank them; and would send them back the plague, / Could I but catch it for them.
I thank them, and I'd send them back the plague, if I could catch it for them.

O! forget / What we are sorry for ourselves in thee. / The senators with one consent of love / Entreat thee back to Athens, who have thought / On special dignities, which vacant lie / For thy best use and wearing.

Oh, forget what we ourselves are sorry for having done to you. The senators, united in love, beg you to come back to Athens. They have set aside special honours, which lie vacant for you to use and wear.

They confess / Toward thee forgetfulness too general, gross; / Which now the public body, which doth seldom / Play the recanter, feeling in itself / A lack of Timon's aid, hath sense withal / Of it own fail, restraining aid to Timon, / And send forth us to make their sorrow'd render, / Together with a recompense more fruitful / Than their offence can weigh down by the dram; / Ay, even such heaps and sums of love and wealth / As shall to thee blot out what wrongs were theirs, / And write in thee the figures of their love, / Ever to read them thine.

They confess they forgot you too widely and grossly. Now the state, which seldom takes back what it has done, feeling the lack of Timon's help, also recognises its own failure in withholding help from Timon. It has sent us to express its sorrow, together with a reward richer than their offence could outweigh by even a grain: yes, such heaps and sums of love and wealth as will wipe out the wrongs they did you and write their love in you in figures you can always read as yours.
You witch me in it; / Surprise me to the very brink of tears. / Lend me a fool's heart and a woman's eyes, / And I'll beweep these comforts, worthy senators.
You bewitch me with this. You surprise me to the very edge of tears. Lend me a fool's heart and a woman's eyes, and I'll weep over these comforts, worthy senators.

Therefore so please thee to return with us, / And of our Athens—thine and ours—to take / The captainship, thou shalt be met with thanks, / Allow'd with absolute power, and thy good name / Live with authority. So soon we shall drive back / Of Alcibiades the approaches wild, / Who, like a boar too savage, doth root up / His country's peace.

So, if you will come back with us and take command of our Athens, yours and ours, you'll be met with thanks, given absolute power, and your good name will live with authority. Then we'll soon drive back the wild attacks of Alcibiades, who, like a savage boar, is rooting up his country's peace.
And shakes his threat'ning sword / Against the walls of Athens.
And shakes his threatening sword at the walls of Athens.

Well, sir, I will. Therefore I will, sir, thus: / If Alcibiades kill my countrymen, / Let Alcibiades know this of Timon, / That Timon cares not. But if he sack fair Athens, / And take our goodly aged men by the beards, / Giving our holy virgins to the stain / Of contumelious, beastly, mad-brain'd war, / Then let him know, and tell him Timon speaks it, / In pity of our aged and our youth / I cannot choose but tell him that I care not, / And let him take't at worst; for their knives care not / While you have throats to answer. For myself, / There's not a whittle in the unruly camp / But I do prize it at my love before / The reverend'st throat in Athens. So I leave you / To the protection of the prosperous gods, / As thieves to keepers.

Well, sir, I will. Therefore I will, sir, like this. If Alcibiades kills my countrymen, let Alcibiades know this from Timon: that Timon doesn't care. But if he sacks fair Athens, and takes our fine old men by their beards, and gives our holy virgins up to the stain of insulting, beastly, mad-brained war, then let him know, and tell him Timon says it, that out of pity for our old and our young I cannot help but tell him I don't care. Let him do his worst. Their knives don't care, as long as you have throats to meet them. As for me, there isn't a pocket-knife in that unruly camp that I don't value more than the most respected throat in Athens. So I leave you to the protection of the kindly gods, as thieves are left to their jailers.

Why, I was writing of my epitaph; / It will be seen to-morrow. My long sickness / Of health and living now begins to mend, / And nothing brings me all things. Go, live still; / Be Alcibiades your plague, you his, / And last so long enough!

Why, I was writing my epitaph. It will be seen tomorrow. My long sickness of health and life is now beginning to get better, and nothing will give me everything. Go, live on. May Alcibiades be your plague and you his, and may it last long enough!
But yet I love my country, and am not / One that rejoices in the common wrack, / As common bruit doth put it.
But still I love my country, and I'm not a man who rejoices in its general ruin, as common rumour says.
Commend me to my loving countrymen,—
Give my regards to my loving countrymen...
These words become your lips as they pass through / them.
These words suit your lips as they pass through them.
And enter in our ears like great triumphers / In their applauding gates.
And they enter our ears like great conquerors through gates full of cheering crowds.

Commend me to them, / And tell them that, to ease them of their griefs, / Their fears of hostile strokes, their aches, losses, / Their pangs of love, with other incident throes / That nature's fragile vessel doth sustain / In life's uncertain voyage, I will some kindness do them: / I'll teach them to prevent wild Alcibiades' wrath.

Give them my regards, and tell them that, to ease them of their griefs, their fears of enemy blows, their aches and losses, their pangs of love and the other troubles that nature's fragile ship must suffer on life's uncertain voyage, I will do them a kindness. I'll teach them how to escape wild Alcibiades' anger.
I like this well; he will return again.
I like this. He'll come back with us.

I have a tree, which grows here in my close, / That mine own use invites me to cut down, / And shortly must I fell it. Tell my friends, / Tell Athens, in the sequence of degree / From high to low throughout, that whoso please / To stop affliction, let him take his haste, / Come hither, ere my tree hath felt the axe, / And hang himself. I pray you do my greeting.

I have a tree growing here in my enclosure that I need to cut down for my own use, and I must fell it soon. Tell my friends, tell Athens, in order of rank from highest to lowest, that whoever wants to put an end to his suffering should hurry here, before my tree feels the axe, and hang himself. Please pass on my greeting.
Trouble him no further; thus you still shall find him.
Don't trouble him any more. This is how you'll always find him.

Come not to me again; but say to Athens / Timon hath made his everlasting mansion / Upon the beached verge of the salt flood, / Who once a day with his embossed froth / The turbulent surge shall cover. Thither come, / And let my gravestone be your oracle. / Lips, let sour words go by and language end: / What is amiss, plague and infection mend! / Graves only be men's works and death their gain! / Sun, hide thy beams! Timon hath done his reign.

Don't come to me again, but tell Athens that Timon has made his everlasting home on the beach at the edge of the salt sea, which once a day the stormy waves will cover with their foam. Come there, and let my gravestone be your oracle. Lips, let bitter words pass and let speech end. Whatever is wrong, let plague and infection put it right! Let graves be men's only work, and death their only profit! Sun, hide your beams! Timon's reign is over.
His discontents are unremovably / Coupled to nature.
His discontent is permanently tied to his nature.
Our hope in him is dead. Let us return / And strain what other means is left unto us / In our dear peril.
Our hope in him is dead. Let's go back and try whatever other means we have left in our great danger.
Thou hast painfully discover'd; are his files / As full as thy report?
Your news is painful. Are his ranks as full as you report?
I have spoke the least. / Besides, his expedition promises / Present approach.
I've understated it. And his speed promises he'll be here very soon.
We stand much hazard if they bring not Timon.
We're in great danger if they don't bring Timon back.

I met a courier, one mine ancient friend, / Whom, though in general part we were oppos'd, / Yet our old love had a particular force, / And made us speak like friends. This man was riding / From Alcibiades to Timon's cave / With letters of entreaty, which imported / His fellowship i' the cause against your city, / In part for his sake mov'd.

I met a messenger, an old friend of mine. Although we were on opposite sides in public, our old affection had a private power and made us talk like friends. This man was riding from Alcibiades to Timon's cave with letters begging him to join the campaign against your city, which was partly started for his sake.
No talk of Timon, nothing of him expect. / The enemies' drum is heard, and fearful scouring / Doth choke the air with dust. In, and prepare. / Ours is the fall, I fear; our foes the snare.

Don't talk of Timon; expect nothing from him. The enemy's drum can be heard, and their terrifying raids are choking the air with dust. Inside, and prepare. I'm afraid the fall will be ours, and the trap our enemies'.

By all description this should be the place. / Who's here? Speak, ho! No answer! What is this? / Timon is dead, who hath outstretch'd his span. / Some beast rear'd this; here does not live a man. / Dead, sure; and this his grave. What's on this tomb / I cannot read; the character I'll take with wax. / Our captain hath in every figure skill, / An ag'd interpreter, though young in days; / Before proud Athens he's set down by this, / Whose fall the mark of his ambition is.

By every description this should be the place. Who's here? Hello, speak! No answer! What's this? Timon is dead; he has lived out his span. Some beast built this; no man lives here. Dead, certainly, and this is his grave. I can't read what's written on this tomb. I'll take an impression of the letters in wax. Our captain can read every kind of writing; he's an old interpreter, though young in years. By now he'll have laid siege to proud Athens, whose fall is the target of his ambition.
Sound to this coward and lascivious town / Our terrible approach.
Let the trumpets announce our terrible approach to this cowardly, lustful town.

Till now you have gone on and fill'd the time / With all licentious measure, making your wills / The scope of justice; till now, myself, and such / As slept within the shadow of your power, / Have wander'd with our travers'd arms, and breath'd / Our sufferance vainly. Now the time is flush, / When crouching marrow, in the bearer strong, / Cries of itself, 'No more!' Now breathless wrong / Shall sit and pant in your great chairs of ease, / And pursy insolence shall break his wind / With fear and horrid flight.

Until now you have gone on filling your time with every kind of licence, making your own wishes the limit of justice. Until now, I and those who lived in the shadow of your power have wandered with folded arms and breathed out our sufferings in vain. Now the time is ripe, when the crouching spirit, grown strong in the one who bears it, cries out of its own accord "No more!" Now exhausted wrong shall sit panting in your great easy chairs, and fat insolence shall lose its breath in fear and frantic flight.

Noble and young, / When thy first griefs were but a mere conceit, / Ere thou hadst power or we had cause of fear, / We sent to thee, to give thy rages balm, / To wipe out our ingratitude with loves / Above their quantity.

Noble young man, when your first grievances were still only a thought, before you had power or we had reason to fear, we sent to you to soothe your anger and wipe out our ingratitude with greater love than the wrong deserved.
So did we woo / Transformed Timon to our city's love / By humble message and by promis'd means. / We were not all unkind, nor all deserve / The common stroke of war.

In the same way we courted the transformed Timon back to our city's love with humble messages and promises of wealth. We were not all unkind, and we don't all deserve to be struck down together by war.

These walls of ours / Were not erected by their hands from whom / You have receiv'd your griefs; nor are they such / That these great towers, trophies, and schools, should fall / For private faults in them.
These walls of ours weren't built by the hands of the men who wronged you, and the wrongs aren't such that these great towers, monuments and schools should fall for the private faults of a few.

Nor are they living / Who were the motives that you first went out; / Shame, that they wanted cunning, in excess / Hath broke their hearts. March, noble lord, / Into our city with thy banners spread. / By decimation and a tithed death,— / If thy revenges hunger for that food / Which nature loathes,—take thou the destin'd tenth, / And by the hazard of the spotted die / Let die the spotted.

And the men who first caused you to leave are no longer alive. Shame at their lack of foresight has broken their hearts. March into our city, noble lord, with your banners flying. If your revenge hungers for the food that nature hates, then kill one in every ten, take the tenth man fate assigns you, and by the chance of the spotted dice let the spotted, the guilty, die.

All have not offended; / For those that were, it is not square to take, / On those that are, revenge: crimes, like lands, / Are not inherited. Then, dear countryman, / Bring in thy ranks, but leave without thy rage; / Spare thy Athenian cradle, and those kin / Which, in the bluster of thy wrath, must fall / With those that have offended. Like a shepherd / Approach the fold and cull th' infected forth, / But kill not all together.

Not everyone has offended. It isn't fair to take revenge on those who are alive for the sake of those who are gone. Crimes, unlike lands, aren't inherited. So, dear countryman, bring in your soldiers but leave your anger outside. Spare your Athenian birthplace and those relatives who, in the storm of your anger, would fall along with the guilty. Like a shepherd, go into the fold and pick out the infected sheep, but don't kill them all together.
What thou wilt, / Thou rather shalt enforce it with thy smile / Than hew to 't with thy sword.
Whatever you want, you'll achieve it more easily with your smile than by hacking your way to it with your sword.
Set but thy foot / Against our rampir'd gates and they shall ope, / So thou wilt send thy gentle heart before / To say thou'lt enter friendly.
Just set your foot against our fortified gates and they'll open, as long as you send your gentle heart ahead to say you'll come in as a friend.

Throw thy glove, / Or any token of thine honour else, / That thou wilt use the wars as thy redress / And not as our confusion, all thy powers / Shall make their harbour in our town till we / Have seal'd thy full desire.

Throw down your glove, or any other token of your honour, to show you'll use this war to set right your wrongs and not to destroy us, and all your forces shall be housed in our town until we have met all your demands.

Then there's my glove; / Descend, and open your uncharged ports. / Those enemies of Timon's and mine own, / Whom you yourselves shall set out for reproof, / Fall, and no more. And, to atone your fears / With my more noble meaning, not a man / Shall pass his quarter or offend the stream / Of regular justice in your city's bounds, / But shall be render'd to your public laws / At heaviest answer.

Then there's my glove. Come down and open your gates, which haven't been attacked. Only those enemies of Timon's and of mine whom you yourselves pick out for punishment shall die, and no more. And to settle your fears with my nobler intentions, not one of my men shall leave his quarters or break the course of ordinary justice within your city's bounds without being handed over to your public laws for the heaviest punishment.
Come down, and keep your promises.

My noble General, Timon is dead; / Entomb'd upon the very hem o' the sea; / And on his gravestone this insculpture, which / With wax I brought away, whose soft impression / Interprets for my poor ignorance.

My noble general, Timon is dead, buried on the very edge of the sea. And on his gravestone is this inscription. I've brought away an impression of it in soft wax, which can speak for my poor ignorance.

[Reads the epitaph] 'Here lies a wretched corse, of wretched soul bereft; / Seek not my name. A plague consume you wicked caitiffs left! / Here lie I, Timon, who alive all living men did hate. / Pass by, and curse thy fill; but pass, and stay not here thy gait.' / These well express in thee thy latter spirits. / Though thou abhorr'dst in us our human griefs, / Scorn'dst our brain's flow, and those our droplets which / From niggard nature fall, yet rich conceit / Taught thee to make vast Neptune weep for aye / On thy low grave, on faults forgiven. Dead / Is noble Timon, of whose memory / Hereafter more. Bring me into your city, / And I will use the olive with my sword; / Make war breed peace, make peace stint war, make each / Prescribe to other, as each other's leech. / Let our drums strike.

(Reads the epitaph) "Here lies a wretched body, robbed of its wretched soul. Do not look for my name. May a plague destroy you wicked wretches who are left! Here I lie, Timon, who hated all living men while I was alive. Pass by and curse as much as you like, but pass by, and do not stop here." These words express well your feelings at the end. Though you hated our human sorrows and scorned the tears that fall in small drops from stingy nature, your rich imagination taught you to make vast Neptune weep forever on your humble grave for faults forgiven. Noble Timon is dead, and of his memory we shall say more later. Take me into your city, and I will use the olive branch together with my sword. I will make war produce peace, and peace limit war, and make each the doctor of the other. Let our drums strike up.
